Yes, I’ve been missing in action for a few days . . . I was needed elsewhere for family stuff and left my laptop behind!![Image 49: 😂](https://s0.wp.com/wp-content/mu-plugins/wpcom-smileys/twemoji/2/svg/1f602.svg)![Image 50: 🤣](https://s0.wp.com/wp-content/mu-plugins/wpcom-smileys/twemoji/2/svg/1f923.svg)

I have received four new NetGalley ARCs in the past week and have taken out one library book as my ‘read for pleasure’.

My library book is Close to Death, #5 in the Hawthorne & Horowitz series by Anthony Horowitz, Close to Death.

![Image 51](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/close-to-death.jpg?w=344)
Riverside Close is a picture-perfect community. The six exclusive and attractive houses are tucked far away from the noise and grime of city life, allowing the residents to enjoy beautiful gardens, pleasant birdsong and tranquility from behind the security of a locked gate.

It is the perfect idyll until the Kentworthy family arrives, with their four giant, gas-guzzling cars, a gaggle of shrieking children and plans for a garish swimming pool in the backyard. Obvious outsiders, the Kentworthys do not belong in Riverside Close, and they quickly offend every last one of their neighbours.

When Giles Kentworthy is found dead on his own doorstep, a crossbow bolt sticking out of his chest, Detective Hawthorne is the only investigator that can be called on to solve the case.

Because how do you solve a murder when everyone is a suspect?

My NetGalley ARCs are Evensong by Stewart O’Nan. I have previously read and enjoyed Ocean State by this author.

![Image 52](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/evensong.png?w=255)
**An intimate, moving novel that follows The Humpty Dumpty Club, a group of women of a certain age who band together to help one another and their circle of friends in Pittsburgh as they face the challenges of their golden years**

The Humpty Dumpty Club is distraught when its powerhouse leader, Joan Hargrove, takes a bad fall down her stairs, knocking her out of commission. Now, as well as running errands and shepherding those less able to their doctors’ appointments, the club members have to pick up the slack.

Between navigating their own relationships and aging bodies and attending choir practice, these invisible yet indomitable women help where they can. They bake cookies, they care for pets, they pick up prescriptions, they sit vigil by the sick, and most of all, they show up for the people they’ve pledged to help. In the face of death, divorce, and the myriad directions our lives can take, the Humpty Dumpty club represents the power of community and chosen family.

I picked up a backtitle audiobook from Charles Martin – When Crickets Cry. This was published in 2019 but is still available on NetGalley.

![Image 53](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/when-crickets-cry.png?w=255)
It begins on the shaded town square in a sleepy Southern town. A spirited seven-year-old has a brisk business at her lemonade stand. But the little girl’s pretty yellow dress can’t quite hide the ugly scar on her chest.

Her latest customer, a bearded stranger, drains his cup and heads to his car, his mind on a boat he’s restoring at a nearby lake. The stranger understands more about the scar than he wants to admit. And the beat-up bread truck careening around the corner with its radio blaring is about to change the trajectory of both their lives.

Before it’s over, they’ll both know there are painful reasons why crickets cry . . . and that miracles lurk around unexpected corners.

I have read a few books by Alex Gray now and enjoyed them all. Acts of Malice is her latest (published a few days ago).

![Image 54](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/acts-of-malice.png)
DSI William Lorimer first meets Meredith St Claire when he is giving a careers talk at his goddaughter’s school. The popular and glamorous drama teacher is distraught, begging him to investigate her fiancé’s recent disappearance, but with a report already made to the relevant authorities, there’s nothing more Lorimer can do.  
But then a body is discovered on the outskirts of Glasgow.

Guy Richmond was a wealthy and charismatic actor, adored by everyone. Or so it first seems. But as Lorimer and his team are drawn deeper into the peculiar world of professional theatre, they find themselves caught in a web of confidences and rivalry, thwarted dreams and ruthless ambition.

For it seems the finest actors of all are those with the darkest secrets to hide.

Cockatoo Cove will be my second book by Australia author Maya Linnell.

![Image 55](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/cockatoo-cove.png?w=255)
Maggie West has worked her entire adult life to prove herself, establishing a successful cattle stud instead of following her father into the crayfishing industry, though it’s never enough to stop local speculation about her family’s holdings. And with her teenage daughter close to veering off the rails, she knows all too well that money doesn’t provide immunity against heartache or hardship.

Since landing in South Australia’s picturesque Limestone Coast, Scottish winemaker Fergus Abernathy has gone from strength to strength. But it isn’t just the awards or his stint as an unlikely social media superstar that’s keeping him in the district; if he can put down roots, perhaps he can persuade his family to join him Down Under.

Missing his family back in Scotland, Fergus looks a little enviously at the close-knit West family, until a shocking phone call changes everything.

Misunderstandings, scams and long-withheld secrets create roadblocks for Maggie and Fergus, and with a community fundraiser hanging in the balance, it seems they’re never destined to be in the right place at the right time.

I have five new NetGalley ARCs this week, plus one audiobook of a title I already have the e-book of, so I am not counting that as an addition.

Of my five new reads, two are audiobooks:

Sisters by Kellie Coates Gilbert, a new to me author, and narrated by E.L. Beckett.

![Image 60](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/sisters.png?w=255)
**Sisters celebrates the joys and heartaches shared by three sisters living in the mountain resort known as Sun Valley, the mistakes made in the name of love and the healing power of new beginnings.**

**Karyn Macadam**is starting over after losing her husband to a skiing accident. A chance encounter with a backcountry pilot might be this young widow’s one shot at a new beginning, but only if she can let go of the past.

**Leigh Ann Blackburn**is the perfect wife, until her husband grows more distant and she believes the worst. An outrageous plan to save her marriage turns the situation on its head and she soon learns not everything is as it seems.

**Joie Abbott**, who always finds a way to mess up her life, has done it yet again. This time a bitter betrayal threatens to expose a heartache she desperately wants to keep secret, especially from her family.

Through romance and heartbreak, laughter and tears . . .  
life is always better with your sisters at your side.

My second audiobook is No Comfort for the Dead written by R.P. O’Donnell and narrated by Nicola F. Delgardo.

![Image 61](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/no-comfort-for-the-dead.png?w=255)
**After witnessing a murder, a small-town librarian is forced to act when the local police arrest the wrong man**.

1988, West Cork, Ireland.Emma Daly has returned to her home in Castlefreke, a small and peaceful village where everybody knows everybody. She has taken over the local library and is trying not to think about the scandal she left behind in the city. But when the richest man in the village is murdered and the main suspect is the mysterious son of a local family, her charming small-town life is turned upside down.

Emma knows for a fact that there is more to the story, and when the family asks her to investigate, she decides to take matters into her own hands.

Teaming up with a stubborn widow, an elderly hypochondriac, and her high school sweetheart, it is up to Emma to solve the mystery before either the police or the murderer can stop her.

My three new e-ARCs are:

The Obsessions of Harvey Usher by David Putnam.

![Image 62](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/the-obsessions-of-harvey-ussher.png?w=255)
At eighty years old, Harvey Usher lives a quiet, reclusive life, still grieving the loss of his beloved wife, Sylvia. But when a stunning redhead named Rita shows up, claiming to be his wife of two years, Harvey’s carefully constructed world begins to crumble.

As Harvey struggles to expose Rita’s deception, dark figures from his past emerge from the shadows, forcing him to confront the violent secrets he’s kept buried for five decades. With the help of his elderly neighbor Esther and a troubled PI named Eddie Gurski, Harvey races to uncover Rita’s true motives before it’s too late.

But in this deadly game of cat and mouse, nothing is what it seems. As bodies start piling up and long-buried truths come to light, Harvey must decide who he can trust—and whether some sins can ever truly be forgiven.

The Oasis by Anne Buist and Graeme Simsion, which picks up trainee psychiatrist Hannah Wright’s life where The Glass House finished.

![Image 63](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/the-oasis.png?w=255)
Trainee psychiatrist**Doctor Hannah Wright**has only just got her head above water in the acute psychiatric ward at Menzies Hospital when she’s thrown into the deep end of the outpatient clinic. Keen to develop her skills in talking therapies, she finds herself up against a boss who’s focused on medication and a senior colleague with a score to settle.

Hannah’s fellow first-years face problems of their own: on-and-off flame**Alex**is being bullied,**Ndidi**‘s marriage is in trouble,**Jon**feels isolated and**Carey**is concerned their autism will be a career barrier.

While Hannah comes under pressure to seek therapy herself to confront a traumatic past, her patients’ health issues range from OCD to ice addiction, childhood abuse to the mental impact of ageing, and from bad parenting to bad genes. They all come to the Oasis.

And Barren Cape by Michelle Prak.

![Image 64](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/barren-cape.png?w=255)
**An abandoned resort seems the perfect place to hide, but is Barren Cape a refuge or a trap?**  
  
Former housemates Mac and Erika are homeless.  
  
Well, Erika is fine, she just has to live with her parents until she can find another rental. Mac’s situation is much worse – family isn’t an option and she’s surfing the couches of her increasingly exasperated friends.  
  
Driving around one lonely afternoon, Mac discovers Barren Cape. Once destined to be a luxury escape, now it’s just wire fence and gray cement.

It’s stark, but quiet. There’s no harm in staying a little while…

## [The Sun’s Shadow by Sejal Badani](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/2025/02/06/the-suns-shadow-by-sejal-badani/)

![Image 66](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/the-suns-shadow.png?w=255)
EXCERPT: Felicity  
_‘Celine’s father left when she was six,’ Elena interrupts. Her voice, quiet and unassuming, conceals a steely demeanor. ‘Packed his bags and we never saw him again.’  
Shocked by the information, I wonder why Eric never mentioned it to me.  
‘As a mother, all I could think of was how to protect my child. To make sure, with everything happening, that she was safe and taken care of.’  
I don’t want to hear about Celine’s childhood or her struggles. I don’t want to think about the woman I betrayed as anything but a body, a person who’s gotten to love and me married to Justin’s father.  
‘I imagine you felt the same with Justin.’  
‘Yes.’ My spine straightens, bringing me to my full height. ‘He’s always been my main priority.’  
‘A child knows when they’ve been loved,’ Elena says. ‘It explains why he is who he is.’ She leans against the pillar, seeking support. ‘As a mother, when our back is against the wall, we will do anything to protect our child.’ Elena looks me right in the eyes. ‘You did what you had to do. But now, allowing Justing to be tested, you’re stepping forward to protect my grandson. I won’t forget this.’  
I stare at her, taken aback. It was the last thing I expected when the conversation began. But it also drives home that these are real people, with real emotions and events in their lives. Elena’s pass on the past offers the necessary relief from guilt or responsibility. I nod, accepting her gratitude. But a small voice inside my head balks at the idea. I say my goodbyes, the ghosts of my choices fast on my heels._

ABOUT ‘THE SUN’S SHADOW’: Celine’s life is spiraling out of control. She’s in danger of losing the beloved equestrian farm that was her childhood home. Her distant husband, Eric, is devoting a suspicious amount of time to a stunning new colleague. Then her young son, Brian, receives a devastating cancer diagnosis. How much worse can things get?

Felicity has uprooted her career and her teenage son, Justin, to get closer to Eric. She’s tired of keeping his secrets—that Justin is his son, and Eric’s frequent “business trips” have been spent playing the good dad with him. Felicity is determined to get her happily ever after, even if it means confronting Celine at a delicate time.

But when Brian’s prognosis worsens, and a transplant from Justin becomes his best chance at survival, Felicity must make a wrenching decision about her son’s well-being—and Celine must accept that the “other woman” is her only hope.

In another life Celine and Felicity might have been friends. Can they put aside the pain between them to do what’s best for their families—and their own futures?

MY THOUGHTS: I am obviously alone on outlier island with my thoughts on and feelings about The Sun’s Shadow by Sejal Badani.

The premise is wonderful, and I went into this read expecting my emotions to overflow but I found the writing stilted and unwieldy. I was unable to get my teeth into the narrative. I could not relate to any of the characters except Justin and Brian. And even then, I wondered how realistically they were portrayed. It would be nice if all teenagers and pre-teens were like this, but I personally don’t know any who are.

I threw up my hands in despair at some of Celine’s decisions and actions.

And just what was Felicity thinking? Yes, I could understand she wanted to be with Eric, but the status of their personal relationship over the year seems to have revolved entirely around Justin and, please correct me if I am wrong, nothing else. Although this is not explicitly stated and I don’t believe Celine actually asked the question, that is the impression I am left with.[(hide spoiler)]

There is a lot of angst and introspection and, indeed, repetition that eventually caused me to skim read large tracts.

Everyone else appears to have loved this The Sun’s Shadow, so maybe it is just me who is left feeling dissatisfied after reading it. Please check out some of the other more positive reviews.

## [The Glass House by Anne Buist and Graeme Simsion](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/2025/01/24/the-glass-house-by-anne-buist-and-graeme-simsion/)

![Image 70](https://sandysbookaday.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/the-glass-house.png?w=255)
EXCERPT:_It’s an unremarkable Victorian terrace in an inner suburb of Melbourne. Only the closed curtains on a summer morning suggest that anything is amiss.  
Behind them, the open living space is in disarray. Household items are scattered on the floor: cooking pots, cleaning products, a baby’s rattle. But there has been method in their placement. Below the sink, three rows of tinned food mark the start of a trail that runs to the front door: literal stumbling blocks for an intruder who wanted to take the shortest route to the kitchen bench.  
A woman – small, dark-haired and visibly agitated – enters from the back garden in her dressing-gown, carrying a pot plant. She deposits it in the hallway outside the nursery, then fetches a stool from the kitchen. She climbs up with the plant and balances it on top of the door.  
A laugh – unnatural, fractured – escapes her. It’s partly the image of the booby-trap going off, partly a perverse satisfaction that they’ve chosen the wrong woman to mess with and, perhaps, the only way her mind can deal with what she has to do next.  
Back in the kitchen, the baby carrier is sitting on the bench. Matilda was crying all night and now she’s crying again. Sian pulls a kitchen knife from the block._

ABOUT ‘THE GLASS HOUSE’: Psychiatry registrar Doctor Hannah Wright, a country girl with a chaotic history, thought she had seen it all in the emergency room. But that was nothing compared to the psychiatric ward at Menzies Hospital.

Hannah must learn on the job in a strained medical system, as she and her fellow trainees deal with the common and the bizarre, the hilarious and the tragic, the treatable and the confronting. Every day brings new patients: Chloe, who has a life-threatening eating disorder; Sian, suffering postpartum psychosis and fighting to keep her baby; and Xavier, the MP whose suicide attempt has an explosive story behind it. All the while, Hannah is trying to figure out herself.

MY THOUGHTS: I started The Glass House not knowing what to expect, but I am thoroughly impressed by its realism and honesty. Having worked in the mental health field for a number of years as a psychiatric nurse, I know there is no one answer, no guarantees and, especially when a patient is being discharged back into the same circumstances they were admitted from, often precious little hope.

For me, The Glass House was like a trip down memory lane. The infighting and one-upmanship so prevalent amongst the consultants, each with their own pet therapies they prefer and push, and their favored staff members. Other staff are either berated or ignored.

Psychiatric medicine is not a case of one size (or treatment) fits all, and this is well-illustrated in The Glass House. Each case is unique – no two minds work the same even given the same set of circumstances.

I liked the format of this book. Each chapter starts with a biopic of a psychiatric crisis prior to the patient’s admission to hospital. Then we are privy to the patient’s journey accompanied by one member, or sometimes more, of the diverse staff on the psych ward.

Hannah Wright, Psychiatric Registrar, is our main character. As so often is the case in this profession, she has a trauma in her background, and it is this that led her to her choice of career path. But at the same time, she is having a crisis of faith in herself. Is psychiatry the right path for her? Or should she return to general medicine where she knows with certainty that she can save lives?

Anne Buist and Graeme Simsion have written an honest and engaging novel, a book with both wit and wisdom and one that eloquently illustrates just how frail and how strong humans are. I look forward to reading more from this couple. The Glass House has a permanent place on my ‘forever’ shelf.

109 Strange Things Korean Drama
[**KDRAMALOVE KOREAN DRAMA REVIEWS**](https://www.kdramalove.com/reviews.html)  
  
![Image 1](https://www.kdramalove.com/Its-Okay-not-to-be-okay.jpg)  
  
**It's Okay To Not Be Okay**  
**사이코지만 괜찮아**  
 Studio Dragon (2020) 16 Episodes  
 Family Medical Melodrama, **Grade: B-**  
 Korean Drama Review by Jill, USA  
_(Some Spoilers)_  
  
 ~~~~~~~~~  

> > > I really wanted to like this family medical drama **It's Okay To Not Be Okay** (2020) because its male star Kim Soo Hyun ([**My Love From Anot****her Star**](https://www.kdramalove.com/mylovestar.html), [**Dream High**](https://www.kdramalove.com/DreamHigh.html), [**Father's House**](https://www.kdramalove.com/FathersHouse.html), etc.) is an actor I have always enjoyed watching over the years, dating back to his earliest works when he was first getting into show biz. This was his first starring role in a drama since he was released from his military requirement and I wanted to support his work. It turned out to be far more difficult for me to do that as the story progressed. I stayed the course and finished it, but it felt like enduring a hurting pulled tooth; it's definitely not his best drama, not by a long shot. That honor remains with the superlative masterpiece [**My Love From Another Star**](https://www.kdramalove.com/mylovestar.html). That one will stand the test of time, and this one will soon be forgotten (and I'm sure deep down he knows that, too). Even the title of this drama makes little sense. If **you** were not okay, would you still think that was a perfectly fine way to continue living your life? Wouldn't you **want** to be okay instead? Even the original title was weird: _I'm A Psycho, But That's Okay_. If **you** were a psycho, would you consider that to be an okay way to live? I doubt it. Everyone wants to be **normal**. Everyone wants to be **okay**. The title here _should_ have been **It's Not Okay To Be A Psycho**. That at least would have given these mentally troubled characters a positive goal to shoot for!   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 2](https://www.kdramalove.com/KimSooHyun_its-okay-to-not-be-okay.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > _Kim Soo Hyun_  
> > >   
> > > 
> > > The first few episodes I did rather enjoy, even though I had some reservations about the story and the characters from the very start, but as the drama progressed it became harder and harder for me to tolerate it, or to even like the characters much. It just became tedious. Definitely the fault of the writer of the script, someone who had only written one prior drama, and who obviously didn't quite know how to create an exceptional story instead of a superficial, trite, campy, predictable, frustrating, cliche-ridden one. There didn't seem to be much real personal growth in the characters for the majority of the story, either: people who were all severely wounded mentally, stemming from their sad, love-starved childhoods (a favorite theme of many Korean dramas and films). And of course the three main lead characters knew each other briefly in childhood. Excuse me if I yawn over that vastly overused trope as well.   
> > >   
> > >  The fact that one of the characters, an adult male, was severely autistic (actor Oh Jung Se, [**When The Camellia Blooms**](https://www.kdramalove.com/CamelliaBlooms.html)), and not really receiving proper medical care for his condition, bothered me quite a bit, since I am a mother who raised a child on the autism spectrum, and worked very hard to get that child to finish high school, and even to get a college degree and become independent. The autistic-savant character here in this drama had some artistic talents that could have been a key to help him live a more normal life, but no one around him, not even his loving brother played by Kim Soo Hyun, really encouraged him to develop that talent from youth in any steady, meaningful way.   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 3](https://www.kdramalove.com/oh-jung-se-its-okay-to-not-be-okay.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > _Oh Jung Se_  
> > > 
> > > Then they threw into the mix of the two brothers' story a female lead character, played by Seo Ye Ji ([**Lawless Lawyer**](https://www.kdramalove.com/LawlessLawyer.html)), who was a total outlandish nutcase, a profound narcissist who always had to have things her way or she'd pout and walk off like a spoiled child. She was a character who should have been humbled early on in the story, but who was allowed to trounce upon everyone's feelings for far too long, acting more like an entitled, nasty rich princess living in a luxurious tower, rather than a normal, caring woman with both feet planted firmly on the ground.   
> > >   
> > >  I had found it hard to warm to this actress very much in [**Lawless Lawyer**](https://www.kdramalove.com/LawlessLawyer.html) too, at least in the beginning, so I was prepared to be aspatient as possible with her this time too, but honestly I never really liked her character at all. I tried, but all along I thought Kim Soo Hyun's character would have been **far** better served by having a helpmeet like the normal girl who had a crush on him for years, played by the second female lead, Park Kyu Young, who was a total sweetie. In real life a couple like the one played by Kim Soo Hyun and Seo Ye Ji would never last. They both were far too troubled in their basic natures. I really think that the heart of this drama was the two brothers' story, and that adding a twisted romance detracted from what could have been a unique and special K-drama instead. I felt in a similar way about the 2015 K-drama [**I Remember You**](https://www.kdramalove.com/IRememberYou.html). In that one the two brothers' story (Park Bo Gum and Seo In Guk) was _far_ more interesting than any fluffy romance they tried to bring into the basic story. Although at least in that story Jang Nara's character was a normal working woman, not a rich, entitled witch who wore ridiculously ornate designer clothes and earrings, and strutted around like the world owed her a living and that everyone should serve her because she was just soooo special and rich. Shudder.   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 4](https://www.kdramalove.com/its-okay-to-not-be-okay-episode-9-3.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > _Kim Soo Hyun & Seo Ye Ji_  
> > > 
> > > 
> > > **The Story**:   
> > >   
> > > Brothers Moon Kang Tae (Kim Soo Hyun) and Moon Sang Tae (Oh Jung Se) are loving brothers who have been living and struggling together basically since childhood when their family disintegrated. Kang Tae has to especially watch over his older brother because he is severely autistic and really requires constant watching so that he doesn't harm himself. For instance, due to a trauma in childhood, whenever Sang Tae sees a butterfly he panics and hides himself from anyone who could help him, screaming like a tortured animal. It takes Kang Tae hours to help him to calm down. It's no wonder the stress of caring for his autistic brother is overwhelming at times and makes Kang Tae depressed. As an adult it doesn't help much that he is a lowly-paid male nurse working in wards of psychiatric hospitals. All day long Kang Tae works with mental patients and then comes back to an apartment to take care of an autistic brother. Sometimes he has help from his best friend Jo Jae Soo (Kang Ki Doong) who runs a fried chicken cafe, but Kang Tae continues to live a very harsh existence, and one senses someday he will snap emotionally because of all his burdens.   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 5](https://www.kdramalove.com/-Its-Okay-to-Not-be-Okay.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > His brother Sang Tae likes the illustrated novels of a popular children's writer named Ko Moon Young (Seo Ye Ji). Her stories are dark, with Satanic imagery galore in them, so the audience is tipped off ahead of time that she may have a dark soul and be yet another troubled person in this story. _(Personally I would never allow my children to read her kind of books, eek!, to me that would be c_ _hild abuse!_ _)_. Kang Tae tells Sang Tae that he will take him to see her in person at a book signing, but all does not go well, and Moon Young and Kang Tae end up having a very public confrontation.   
> > >   
> > >  Despite that, Moon Young seems intrigued by Kang Tae and likes that he is so handsome. They end up being thrown together by fate on several other occasions, and then when Kang Tae moves with his brother to start work at a different psychiatric hospital he discovers that he will end up seeing Moon Young even more frequently there because Moon Young's own father Ko Dae Hwan (Lee Eol) is a committed patient there. Slowly we begin to note that Moon Young does not like her father very much because in the past he has tried to kill her and supposedly killed her mother! She doesn't really care if he lives or dies.   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 6](https://www.kdramalove.com/thumb22.jpg)  
> > > 
> > >   
> > >  What a mess of a person Kang Tae now has to deal with, on more and more occasions. This "princess", living in an isolated creepy mansion near the hospital, constantly verbally insults him, but then will try and seductively cozy up to him in the same encounter. Kang Tae, despite himself, seems moved by Moon Young's clear psychiatric disorder and her pleas for attention from him. He's obviously so lonely himself that whatever web she spins he is helpless to extricate himself from it entirely. Although a nice normal nurse working at this hospital, named Nam Joo Ri (Park Gyu Young), likes him, he pays her no attention at all, even though she would have made a much more normal match for him, since they both work in the same profession and both have compassion for others. Even so, when have men ever been smart about women? Joo Ri ends up having growing feelings for Moon Young's long-suffering publicist, Lee Sang In (Kim Joo Hun) instead, and he for her. Their growing affection for each other was nice to watch, and Kang Tae really loses out on the far better woman. He seems oblivious to this fact and totally falls for the troubled Moon Young. Joo Ri even had the far better, more normal mother, Kang Sun Duk (played with her usual flair by veteran actress Kim Mi Kyung) who feeds them all on a daily basis while also dishing out bits of wisdom about life. _(Even I wished to have a mother just like her!_ _)._ While all this is happening Sang Tae has been concentrating on painting a mural on the hospital's wall, a commission for pay. That looks like a positive development in his life, but even that is not to last long.   
> > >   
> > >  Even when Kang Tae and Moon Young plan to take a holiday together it doesn't work out. They fight again and break up immediately. The twists and turns in their relationship were extremely annoying to watch. So too is her family situation, which goes from bad to worse when her father's condition deteriorates even more, and her mother turns out to be still alive and - a shock - a longtime nurse at the same psychiatric hospital _(come on, gimme a break!)_ named Park Haeng Ja (veteran actress Jang Young Nam). This is when I really started to check out mentally from this drama. It was all just too much silliness. It felt like the writer was just throwing globs of paint against a wall and hoping a pretty picture would result, but by the end I was yelling with relief, "Thank God this mess is over!" **:)**  
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 7](https://www.kdramalove.com/BB15h5n5.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > 
> > > I would have been far happier with this story if the primary emphasis had been on the brothers' story. That should have remained the foundation of the story, and it would have ended up a unique masterpiece. Kim Soo Hyun and Oh Jung Se did give excellent performances as the brothers who loved and needed each other. How heart-warming it would have been to show those two characters growing together as a family, and dealing with their sad past effectively as time went on, getting qualified psychiatric professional help when they needed it. That would have been an inspiring way to teach the audience about mental dysfunctions, especially autism. Throwing in a campy, unrealistic romance drew away from this possibility big time. Autistic people deserve more understanding than they got here. The writer was clearly out of her element writing about the subject.   
> > >   
> > >  The two best Korean dramas on the subject of mental issues remain 2014's [**It's Okay, That's Love**](https://www.kdramalove.com/ItsOkayThatsLove.html), and 2020's [**Fix You**](https://www.kdramalove.com/FixYou.html). **It's Okay To Not Be Okay**, which ripped off the title of the far superior K-drama to some extent, doesn't come close to these true masterpieces. Watch them instead.

> > > ~~~~~~~  
> > >   
> > > [**HOME TO KOREAN DRAMA REVIEWS**](https://www.kdramalove.com/reviews.html)

> > > I really wanted to like this family medical drama **It's Okay To Not Be Okay** (2020) because its male star Kim Soo Hyun ([**My Love From Anot****her Star**](https://www.kdramalove.com/mylovestar.html), [**Dream High**](https://www.kdramalove.com/DreamHigh.html), [**Father's House**](https://www.kdramalove.com/FathersHouse.html), etc.) is an actor I have always enjoyed watching over the years, dating back to his earliest works when he was first getting into show biz. This was his first starring role in a drama since he was released from his military requirement and I wanted to support his work. It turned out to be far more difficult for me to do that as the story progressed. I stayed the course and finished it, but it felt like enduring a hurting pulled tooth; it's definitely not his best drama, not by a long shot. That honor remains with the superlative masterpiece [**My Love From Another Star**](https://www.kdramalove.com/mylovestar.html). That one will stand the test of time, and this one will soon be forgotten (and I'm sure deep down he knows that, too). Even the title of this drama makes little sense. If **you** were not okay, would you still think that was a perfectly fine way to continue living your life? Wouldn't you **want** to be okay instead? Even the original title was weird: _I'm A Psycho, But That's Okay_. If **you** were a psycho, would you consider that to be an okay way to live? I doubt it. Everyone wants to be **normal**. Everyone wants to be **okay**. The title here _should_ have been **It's Not Okay To Be A Psycho**. That at least would have given these mentally troubled characters a positive goal to shoot for!   
> > >   
> > >

> > > 
> > > The first few episodes I did rather enjoy, even though I had some reservations about the story and the characters from the very start, but as the drama progressed it became harder and harder for me to tolerate it, or to even like the characters much. It just became tedious. Definitely the fault of the writer of the script, someone who had only written one prior drama, and who obviously didn't quite know how to create an exceptional story instead of a superficial, trite, campy, predictable, frustrating, cliche-ridden one. There didn't seem to be much real personal growth in the characters for the majority of the story, either: people who were all severely wounded mentally, stemming from their sad, love-starved childhoods (a favorite theme of many Korean dramas and films). And of course the three main lead characters knew each other briefly in childhood. Excuse me if I yawn over that vastly overused trope as well.   
> > >   
> > >  The fact that one of the characters, an adult male, was severely autistic (actor Oh Jung Se, [**When The Camellia Blooms**](https://www.kdramalove.com/CamelliaBlooms.html)), and not really receiving proper medical care for his condition, bothered me quite a bit, since I am a mother who raised a child on the autism spectrum, and worked very hard to get that child to finish high school, and even to get a college degree and become independent. The autistic-savant character here in this drama had some artistic talents that could have been a key to help him live a more normal life, but no one around him, not even his loving brother played by Kim Soo Hyun, really encouraged him to develop that talent from youth in any steady, meaningful way.   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 3](https://www.kdramalove.com/oh-jung-se-its-okay-to-not-be-okay.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > _Oh Jung Se_  
> > > 
> > > Then they threw into the mix of the two brothers' story a female lead character, played by Seo Ye Ji ([**Lawless Lawyer**](https://www.kdramalove.com/LawlessLawyer.html)), who was a total outlandish nutcase, a profound narcissist who always had to have things her way or she'd pout and walk off like a spoiled child. She was a character who should have been humbled early on in the story, but who was allowed to trounce upon everyone's feelings for far too long, acting more like an entitled, nasty rich princess living in a luxurious tower, rather than a normal, caring woman with both feet planted firmly on the ground.   
> > >   
> > >  I had found it hard to warm to this actress very much in [**Lawless Lawyer**](https://www.kdramalove.com/LawlessLawyer.html) too, at least in the beginning, so I was prepared to be aspatient as possible with her this time too, but honestly I never really liked her character at all. I tried, but all along I thought Kim Soo Hyun's character would have been **far** better served by having a helpmeet like the normal girl who had a crush on him for years, played by the second female lead, Park Kyu Young, who was a total sweetie. In real life a couple like the one played by Kim Soo Hyun and Seo Ye Ji would never last. They both were far too troubled in their basic natures. I really think that the heart of this drama was the two brothers' story, and that adding a twisted romance detracted from what could have been a unique and special K-drama instead. I felt in a similar way about the 2015 K-drama [**I Remember You**](https://www.kdramalove.com/IRememberYou.html). In that one the two brothers' story (Park Bo Gum and Seo In Guk) was _far_ more interesting than any fluffy romance they tried to bring into the basic story. Although at least in that story Jang Nara's character was a normal working woman, not a rich, entitled witch who wore ridiculously ornate designer clothes and earrings, and strutted around like the world owed her a living and that everyone should serve her because she was just soooo special and rich. Shudder.   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 4](https://www.kdramalove.com/its-okay-to-not-be-okay-episode-9-3.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > _Kim Soo Hyun & Seo Ye Ji_  
> > > 
> > > 
> > > **The Story**:   
> > >   
> > > Brothers Moon Kang Tae (Kim Soo Hyun) and Moon Sang Tae (Oh Jung Se) are loving brothers who have been living and struggling together basically since childhood when their family disintegrated. Kang Tae has to especially watch over his older brother because he is severely autistic and really requires constant watching so that he doesn't harm himself. For instance, due to a trauma in childhood, whenever Sang Tae sees a butterfly he panics and hides himself from anyone who could help him, screaming like a tortured animal. It takes Kang Tae hours to help him to calm down. It's no wonder the stress of caring for his autistic brother is overwhelming at times and makes Kang Tae depressed. As an adult it doesn't help much that he is a lowly-paid male nurse working in wards of psychiatric hospitals. All day long Kang Tae works with mental patients and then comes back to an apartment to take care of an autistic brother. Sometimes he has help from his best friend Jo Jae Soo (Kang Ki Doong) who runs a fried chicken cafe, but Kang Tae continues to live a very harsh existence, and one senses someday he will snap emotionally because of all his burdens.   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 5](https://www.kdramalove.com/-Its-Okay-to-Not-be-Okay.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > His brother Sang Tae likes the illustrated novels of a popular children's writer named Ko Moon Young (Seo Ye Ji). Her stories are dark, with Satanic imagery galore in them, so the audience is tipped off ahead of time that she may have a dark soul and be yet another troubled person in this story. _(Personally I would never allow my children to read her kind of books, eek!, to me that would be c_ _hild abuse!_ _)_. Kang Tae tells Sang Tae that he will take him to see her in person at a book signing, but all does not go well, and Moon Young and Kang Tae end up having a very public confrontation.   
> > >   
> > >  Despite that, Moon Young seems intrigued by Kang Tae and likes that he is so handsome. They end up being thrown together by fate on several other occasions, and then when Kang Tae moves with his brother to start work at a different psychiatric hospital he discovers that he will end up seeing Moon Young even more frequently there because Moon Young's own father Ko Dae Hwan (Lee Eol) is a committed patient there. Slowly we begin to note that Moon Young does not like her father very much because in the past he has tried to kill her and supposedly killed her mother! She doesn't really care if he lives or dies.   
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 6](https://www.kdramalove.com/thumb22.jpg)  
> > > 
> > >   
> > >  What a mess of a person Kang Tae now has to deal with, on more and more occasions. This "princess", living in an isolated creepy mansion near the hospital, constantly verbally insults him, but then will try and seductively cozy up to him in the same encounter. Kang Tae, despite himself, seems moved by Moon Young's clear psychiatric disorder and her pleas for attention from him. He's obviously so lonely himself that whatever web she spins he is helpless to extricate himself from it entirely. Although a nice normal nurse working at this hospital, named Nam Joo Ri (Park Gyu Young), likes him, he pays her no attention at all, even though she would have made a much more normal match for him, since they both work in the same profession and both have compassion for others. Even so, when have men ever been smart about women? Joo Ri ends up having growing feelings for Moon Young's long-suffering publicist, Lee Sang In (Kim Joo Hun) instead, and he for her. Their growing affection for each other was nice to watch, and Kang Tae really loses out on the far better woman. He seems oblivious to this fact and totally falls for the troubled Moon Young. Joo Ri even had the far better, more normal mother, Kang Sun Duk (played with her usual flair by veteran actress Kim Mi Kyung) who feeds them all on a daily basis while also dishing out bits of wisdom about life. _(Even I wished to have a mother just like her!_ _)._ While all this is happening Sang Tae has been concentrating on painting a mural on the hospital's wall, a commission for pay. That looks like a positive development in his life, but even that is not to last long.   
> > >   
> > >  Even when Kang Tae and Moon Young plan to take a holiday together it doesn't work out. They fight again and break up immediately. The twists and turns in their relationship were extremely annoying to watch. So too is her family situation, which goes from bad to worse when her father's condition deteriorates even more, and her mother turns out to be still alive and - a shock - a longtime nurse at the same psychiatric hospital _(come on, gimme a break!)_ named Park Haeng Ja (veteran actress Jang Young Nam). This is when I really started to check out mentally from this drama. It was all just too much silliness. It felt like the writer was just throwing globs of paint against a wall and hoping a pretty picture would result, but by the end I was yelling with relief, "Thank God this mess is over!" **:)**  
> > >   
> > > 
> > > 
> > > 
> > > ![Image 7](https://www.kdramalove.com/BB15h5n5.jpg)  
> > >   
> > > 
> > > I would have been far happier with this story if the primary emphasis had been on the brothers' story. That should have remained the foundation of the story, and it would have ended up a unique masterpiece. Kim Soo Hyun and Oh Jung Se did give excellent performances as the brothers who loved and needed each other. How heart-warming it would have been to show those two characters growing together as a family, and dealing with their sad past effectively as time went on, getting qualified psychiatric professional help when they needed it. That would have been an inspiring way to teach the audience about mental dysfunctions, especially autism. Throwing in a campy, unrealistic romance drew away from this possibility big time. Autistic people deserve more understanding than they got here. The writer was clearly out of her element writing about the subject.   
> > >   
> > >  The two best Korean dramas on the subject of mental issues remain 2014's [**It's Okay, That's Love**](https://www.kdramalove.com/ItsOkayThatsLove.html), and 2020's [**Fix You**](https://www.kdramalove.com/FixYou.html). **It's Okay To Not Be Okay**, which ripped off the title of the far superior K-drama to some extent, doesn't come close to these true masterpieces. How Would Biological Immortality Have Changed the Evolution of Life on Earth?

What would have happened if biological immortality had become widespread among animals during the evolutionary history of life on Earth?

Here, biological immortality means the absence of aging and death from age-related decline, not absolute invulnerability: animals could still die from predators, infections, starvation, injuries, and natural disasters.

For an individual organism, death is the end of life. But in the history of evolution, mortality became one of the factors enabling generational turnover and evolutionary renewal. Paradoxically, the finite lifespans of individual organisms helped make life as a process more resilient to change.

Immortality by itself would not have meant unlimited population growth. Yet a major reduction in mortality would have created a fundamental tension between the lifespan of individuals and the limited carrying capacity of the environment.

Each new generation would add individuals to a population already in existence. If birth rates remained high, population size would quickly approach the limits imposed by available food, water, and territory. Crowding, resource shortages, disease, and intraspecific competition would intensify. In this sense, mortality served as one of the natural checks on overpopulation — an excess of life relative to the carrying capacity of the environment.

Under such conditions, reproduction would come under intense pressure. In many species, energy shortages, chronic stress, and high population density reduce reproductive success. If ecological niches and social positions remained occupied by adult individuals for long periods, younger individuals would also find it more difficult to secure territory, resources, and opportunities to reproduce.

In a population of biologically immortal organisms, maintaining a stable population size would require either that new births be balanced by deaths or emigration, or that reproduction be reduced. The spread of immortality under conditions of limited resources would therefore likely be accompanied by the evolution of mechanisms that sharply restrict reproduction.

An especially important consequence would be a slowdown in generational turnover. Evolution depends on heritable variation, mutations, recombination, and differences in reproductive success. New genetic variants arise and spread across generations. The less frequently generations turn over, the more slowly evolutionary renewal generally proceeds.

Immortality would not stop natural selection: as long as differences in survival and reproduction exist, selection continues to operate. But extreme longevity combined with infrequent reproduction would allow established genotypes to persist for much longer and could slow their replacement by new ones. If the climate changed abruptly, a new pathogen emerged, or another ecological catastrophe occurred, such a population might be less capable of rapid evolutionary adaptation.

There is also an ecological dimension. The death of organisms is an important part of the cycling of matter: decomposition returns carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements to the ecosystem. With a sharp decline in mortality, a substantial share of these elements would remain bound in living biomass for longer, slowing their return to detrital food webs and soil ecosystems. The cycling of matter would not stop completely, since exchange also occurs while organisms are alive, but the structure of ecosystems would change substantially.

Thus, mortality is deeply embedded in the workings of evolution on Earth. It limits overpopulation, frees ecological space, facilitates generational turnover, and plays a role in the cycling of matter. This does not mean that nature deliberately “invented” death for these purposes. Rather, evolution unfolded in a world of mortal organisms, where generational turnover became one of the most important mechanisms of evolutionary renewal.

Here lies a profound paradox: death ends the life of an individual organism, yet the mortality of organisms has contributed to the continuity, capacity for renewal, and adaptability of life as a whole.

Immortality without intelligence and the ability to regulate reproduction, resources, and the state of ecosystems could therefore become not life’s highest victory, but a source of profound crisis.

But with the emergence of intelligence, a new possibility arises. In blind evolution, renewal occurred through generational turnover and the death of individuals. An intelligent civilization could, in principle, try to replace this mechanism with conscious regulation of reproduction, resources, the environment, and its own biological renewal.

Perhaps the central challenge of the future is to preserve individual life while taking over the regulatory and renewal roles that mortality has played for billions of years.

At JSIA, students receive global exposure that goes well beyond what they envision when they join. Since India’s economic and strategic presence is growing worldwide, JSIA tries to match that by blending International Relations, International Law, and International Business in its programmes.

One thing that makes JSIA better is that they start this exposure in the early days of the course. Students who opt for the undergraduate course at JSIA are required to complete three internships within the first five semesters, which pushes them into the real world instead of keeping everything theoretical.

Jindal University’s Office of Career Services helps with this, and they have strong networks with industries across different sectors.

Because of these connections, students get internships and job opportunities with organiszations like Amnesty International, UNDP, Human Rights Watch, BBC Monitoring, Pinkerton, Oxfam, and even universities such as King’s College London.

Global exposure at JSIA goes beyond jobs and internships. The environment is international, with visiting faculty, foreign collaborations, and a strong emphasis on research. Students engage in interdisciplinary, research-driven coursework that encourages global inquiry rather than isolated study.

I'm having trouble with this drama as a Psychology PhD student. I don't want to leave the drama half way through because it has a nice storyline but the depictions on psychological disorders has me on edge sometimes. I can't expect for the writers and director of the drama to be experts in psychology which is why I’m overlooking many things and enjoying the storyline. Still I've watched many psychology Kdramas before and they did a great job in the research, so comparing is inevitable. Getting back to the point, I can't overlook where the storyline is heading.

Antisocial Personality Disorder- commonly known by the terms of sociopathy (raised) and psychopathy (born), it's an irregularity on the brain where neurons are lacking to reproduce hormones that produce emotions. Speaking it's literally a disorder about a lack of emotions- lack of remorse, empathy, etc. There is no cure for this disorder, a person cannot be cured but can become high functioning. High functioning meaning they can live a perfectly normal live between society with the help of therapy, still their brain is structured differently though they can learn how to act according to the situation, they won't feel how the rest feels about the same situation. For example in a funeral they can act accordingly, but that doesn't mean they will necessarily feel sad.

It's important to point out that having this disorder doesn't make anyone a bad person. The majority of assesins and bad people in the world Do Not have this disorder. The guy/girl who played with your emotions and didn't care about you most likely doesn't have this condition either. Society has misinformed and have depicted this disorder with a negative and scary connotation, especially the film industry. High functioning people can live a normal live and won't “harm, kill or manipulate” you as shown in the movies and series, their brain just works differently and lacks emotions.

However, showing a series where they show a person with this disorder falling in love leads to misinformation also. As already said this condition is literally about lacking emotions. Love is a strong feeling, even people without said condition have only fallen in love once in their entire lifetime and others never have. Love requires too much empathy. The moment you love someone, they become the person you feel most empathy for. So people with this condition can't fall in love. They have trouble processing simple feelings, so complex feelings won't happen. This doesn't mean they can't carry on a relationship, but as a couple you would have to understand that they can't fall in love with you, still high functionings know how to act accordingly in a relationship.

I'm still at episode 4 which may be too soon to be commenting lol. If she does fall in love and the writers did their research, I'm leaning towards a wrong diagnosis was given to her and she probably has something else that will become more clear as episodes go by.

Adding to this do not romanticize mental disorders, do not romanticize posessiveness and do not romanticize toxic relationship . DO NOT let people treat you less than good and nice. You aren't someone else's object.

In terms of Itaewon Class, the unpredictability played a huge factor in the distinctive plot. The storyline talks about this young man, Park Sae-ro-yi, facing difficult challenges in life without giving up his righteousness and while starting his own business. It’s hard to predict what new challenges will come his way. Right when you think he will finally succeed and get with his longtime love interest, more roadblocks are piled in front of him and the tables turn once again.

Itaewon Class is actually based on a Webtoon which is not necessarily good or bad. It explains why there is more conflict and action in the show compared to others. That being said, people who do not watch kdrama can enjoy the well written plot as well.

There are many themes. Apart from the main theme of staying strong despite adversities, there are multiple minor hidden themes. For instance, as Kim To-ni is declined from a club for being black, we see some racial injustice prevalent in Korea. By featuring these issues in popular shows, it can hopefully help spread more awareness. After watching this drama, it feels like there are lessons you can take away and apply in your own life.

I have to admit that the Cast in both dramas are nicely selected. Park Seo-joon from Itaewon Class did a great job in portraying his protagonist role. Aside from Lee Joo-young (transgender chef), Kim Dong-hee (illegitimate son) and Park Bo-gum (guest), the other actors are generally not as popular. Disregarding fame, all the actors were quite skilled, allowing the characters to contrast each other perfectly.

![Image 56](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-2abe567c2d131ed8c7c633e46b41b306-lq)

I’m not sure if this is just my experience, but the immense TikTok hype surrounding It’s Okay to Not Be Okay made me enjoy the drama less. It might be because this is many people’s first k-drama. Because, I started watching the show immediately after it was released, nobody knew about it; However, after hearing about everyone else’s opinion, the drama felt extremely hyped near the finale. I would still recommend it though.

It ultimately comes down to which genre of show you prefer more. Itaewon Class is more business, competition, values, food and friendship themed while It’s Okay to Not Be Okay is geared towards romance, psychology, trauma and comedy.

There is a fundamental Korean concept called “Han” 한 (in Hangul). Han is a very complicated emotion to accurately define in English. Some would say it’s impossible to understand if you’re not Korean. The best definition that I can give as someone who has studied Korean language and culture extensively is “a profound mix of grief, longing, resentment, anger, injustice, sadness, and regret”. Han is deeply embedded in Korean culture. The modern definition of Han is largely influenced by the Japanese occupation of Korea from 1910–1945. Families were torn apart politically and geographically. Some elders in Korea still have family in North Korea whom they haven’t seen since the war. It’s truly heart breaking. Han also contains a deep sorrow within it. The feeling of knowing that something isn’t or never will be resolved. This was passed down as a form of generational trauma. Koreans also have a culture-bound mental illness called “Hwabyung” 화병 which literally translates to “anger illness”. Some have claimed people have died from it.

With that in mind, you can see why crying and sadness has become part of many Korean drama storylines. The people who wrote the scripts, produced, directed, acted, etc. in these dramas and movies probably had parents and/or grandparents that lived through the devastation that was brutal colonial rule and post-war Korea. Art can imitate life or aspects of life. This is also why Korea has a huge ballad song catalog.

On another side note, but still relevant I think, is the grieving/funerary culture in Korea. People are encouraged to cry and wail loudly because there is a belief that the tears and cries of the living family members will assist the soul to heaven/afterlife, and because if you don’t show a lot of emotion, people might think you didn’t love whoever it was that passed away very much. This is especially the case if you are the offspring of someone who died. It’s seen as an act of filial piety to grieve openly and loudly. This is in stark contrast to the West (where I’m from) and in Anglo-Saxon, Western European based communities, the conduct at funerals is one of showing perceived strength through/in sadness , silence, remembrance, and reflection. If you cry and wail like Koreans do at funerals in Anglo-Saxon/Western funerals, you’ll be seen as an attention seeker, like you’re trying to prove a point that you’re the saddest person there when clearly everyone there will be sad already. It could also make things worse in an already emotionally unstable life changing event. So yeah, culture differences there too.

Koreans are more emotionally honest, and get headstrong/emotional pretty easily whether it’s something euphoric or upsetting, minor or major. Crying is seen as an act of devotion or care to the person you are crying for/to. It’s exaggerated in dramas for entertainment of course, but nevertheless the sadness and Han roots run deep, and crying in dramas is one manifestation of that.

Why do people like Korean dramas?

Here are some of my reasons:

*   Korean dramas last only one season, usually. This means the season was designed to produce a good story. Not too long; not too short.
*   Korean characters are very well developed. Even the supporting characters have stories to tell. This tends to draw the audience further into the drama.
*   They do romance better than American dramas. With Koreans, love is about a solid relationship where each will stand with the other. It’s not focused on sex like American dramas tend to be.
*   They are very good at comedy and they are very open about things Americans won’t talk about in their dramas, like dog poop and farts, even female ones.
*   The good Korean characters are heavily respectful of others. Of course, the bad characters tend to kick those below them and kiss the ass of those above them. However, this problem is often part of the drama, itself. The bad characters never really win, though.
*   The good Korean characters are very self-reflective about what they may have done that caused something to go wrong. This honesty and sincerity of character is a real draw on viewers, making it possible for them to empathize with them.
*   Music score. The songs or music in the background are almost always good. They weave the drama around you like a blanket, especially in romantic comedies.
*   Korean dramas are almost always partly about family - the effect good or bad on the characters. Koreans are far more family-oriented in almost everything they do when compared to American culture. I like that a lot. Of course, their dramas will show overbearing parents who abuse their children but that is only part of the drama to show how what could have been a good relationship can be so bad.
*   The good Korean characters reframe from using violence whenever they can. They hold it in, and I think that’s better, even though my American English/Irish self many times would have punched the bad character! The Koreans are so much smarter about not adding fuel to someone’s hate and anger.

There are many more reasons but I would have to go into more detail, and most people don’t want that. I just like them so much better than our hard-ass, uncaring, I will kill you American dramas. When we do romance we rarely get it right.

Anyway, Korean dramas are my primary source of entertainment now, along with dramas from China, Taiwan, and Japan. I’m amazed that having the ancestry of the English and Irish that I prefer the Asian culture, the good part of it so much better. At least, for me.

*   Amazing Acting

One of the first things I noticed was the acting in this drama. Both lead actors are extremely versatile and from watching bloopers, you can see how they are really pretty different people in person.

I was personally surprised about his cameo as a delivery guy in Crash Landing on You because his personalities and looks were very diverse. In the drama, he can get the audience quite emotional in certain scenes. His pain is also very evident.

![Image 62](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-2677a3f8687d7c10624582841d6db663-lq)

She has also gained some fame form her dramas S ave Me, Hwarang: The Poet Warrior Youth, Another Miss Oh, and Lawless Lawyer. To me, her character in the drama is a mix of Jo-Yi Seo from Itaewon Class and Wol-joo from Mystic Pop-up Bar; both of which are great developed characters as well.

*   Unique Plot

THIS IS DEFINITELY NOT YOUR TYPICAL ROM-COM K-DRAMA. None of the scenes are cliché at all and there are already many unpredictable moments where you think things would have gone the opposite way. This drama dives deep into the emotional wounds of both characters and is a very emotion-based show in general. The setting is between hospitals and crowds of paparazzi which creates a lot of extra drama. Props to the writers for such a unique plot. This is much more than a simple romance.

![Image 64](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-7234b2205dbfd977f86bb32426a99a52-lq)

*   Touches on Mental Illness

I have heard that in South Korea, mental health is not talked about openly and is generally frowned upon. Despite that, this show is able to touch on mental illness in a more positive light. It shows how people deal with problems differently. Moon Kang-tae’s (male lead) older brother is on the spectrum and it brings to light the difficulties in everyday life for him including panic attacks and public judgement.

The problem with the SaaS Management Platform (SMP) space is that it’s full of point-solutions - some work for Finance teams but don't offer on/offboarding automation for IT; while others are great for IT but bad at optimizing SaaS spend.

Torii approaches it differently by functioning as an all-in-one SaaS Management Platform. Rather than serving just certain teams, it works for the whole organization by excelling in four areas:

1.   Hidden app / Shadow IT discovery - Their discovery process includes API integrations with popular tools, finance connections (QuickBooks, etc.), SSO integrations, and browser extensions.
2.   Spend Optimization - They identify unused licenses and duplicate SaaS spend, making it straightforward to reduce costs.
3.   IT Automation - Their automation workflows streamline onboarding, offboarding, and license management without requiring additional tools.
4.   Contract Renewal Alerts - Their system keeps teams informed about upcoming contract renewals and negotiation windows.

Basically, companies are switching to Torii because they have a SMP that serves the needs of multiple departments, not just IT or Finance.

How Would Biological Immortality Have Changed the Evolution of Life on Earth?

What would have happened if biological immortality had become widespread among animals during the evolutionary history of life on Earth?

Here, biological immortality means the absence of aging and death from age-related decline, not absolute invulnerability: animals could still die from predators, infections, starvation, injuries, and natural disasters.

For an individual organism, death is the end of life. But in the history of evolution, mortality became one of the factors enabling generational turnover and evolutionary renewal. Paradoxically, the finite lifespans of individual organisms helped make life as a process more resilient to change.

Immortality by itself would not have meant unlimited population growth. Yet a major reduction in mortality would have created a fundamental tension between the lifespan of individuals and the limited carrying capacity of the environment.

Each new generation would add individuals to a population already in existence. If birth rates remained high, population size would quickly approach the limits imposed by available food, water, and territory. Crowding, resource shortages, disease, and intraspecific competition would intensify. In this sense, mortality served as one of the natural checks on overpopulation — an excess of life relative to the carrying capacity of the environment.

Under such conditions, reproduction would come under intense pressure. In many species, energy shortages, chronic stress, and high population density reduce reproductive success. If ecological niches and social positions remained occupied by adult individuals for long periods, younger individuals would also find it more difficult to secure territory, resources, and opportunities to reproduce.

In a population of biologically immortal organisms, maintaining a stable population size would require either that new births be balanced by deaths or emigration, or that reproduction be reduced. The spread of immortality under conditions of limited resources would therefore likely be accompanied by the evolution of mechanisms that sharply restrict reproduction.

An especially important consequence would be a slowdown in generational turnover. Evolution depends on heritable variation, mutations, recombination, and differences in reproductive success. New genetic variants arise and spread across generations. The less frequently generations turn over, the more slowly evolutionary renewal generally proceeds.

Immortality would not stop natural selection: as long as differences in survival and reproduction exist, selection continues to operate. But extreme longevity combined with infrequent reproduction would allow established genotypes to persist for much longer and could slow their replacement by new ones. If the climate changed abruptly, a new pathogen emerged, or another ecological catastrophe occurred, such a population might be less capable of rapid evolutionary adaptation.

There is also an ecological dimension. The death of organisms is an important part of the cycling of matter: decomposition returns carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements to the ecosystem. With a sharp decline in mortality, a substantial share of these elements would remain bound in living biomass for longer, slowing their return to detrital food webs and soil ecosystems. The cycling of matter would not stop completely, since exchange also occurs while organisms are alive, but the structure of ecosystems would change substantially.

Thus, mortality is deeply embedded in the workings of evolution on Earth. It limits overpopulation, frees ecological space, facilitates generational turnover, and plays a role in the cycling of matter. This does not mean that nature deliberately “invented” death for these purposes. Rather, evolution unfolded in a world of mortal organisms, where generational turnover became one of the most important mechanisms of evolutionary renewal.

Here lies a profound paradox: death ends the life of an individual organism, yet the mortality of organisms has contributed to the continuity, capacity for renewal, and adaptability of life as a whole.

Immortality without intelligence and the ability to regulate reproduction, resources, and the state of ecosystems could therefore become not life’s highest victory, but a source of profound crisis.

But with the emergence of intelligence, a new possibility arises. In blind evolution, renewal occurred through generational turnover and the death of individuals. An intelligent civilization could, in principle, try to replace this mechanism with conscious regulation of reproduction, resources, the environment, and its own biological renewal.

Perhaps the central challenge of the future is to preserve individual life while taking over the regulatory and renewal roles that mortality has played for billions of years.

At JSIA, students receive global exposure that goes well beyond what they envision when they join. Since India’s economic and strategic presence is growing worldwide, JSIA tries to match that by blending International Relations, International Law, and International Business in its programmes.

One thing that makes JSIA better is that they start this exposure in the early days of the course. Students who opt for the undergraduate course at JSIA are required to complete three internships within the first five semesters, which pushes them into the real world instead of keeping everything theoretical.

Jindal University’s Office of Career Services helps with this, and they have strong networks with industries across different sectors.

Because of these connections, students get internships and job opportunities with organiszations like Amnesty International, UNDP, Human Rights Watch, BBC Monitoring, Pinkerton, Oxfam, and even universities such as King’s College London.

Global exposure at JSIA goes beyond jobs and internships. The environment is international, with visiting faculty, foreign collaborations, and a strong emphasis on research. Students engage in interdisciplinary, research-driven coursework that encourages global inquiry rather than isolated study.

I'm having trouble with this drama as a Psychology PhD student. I don't want to leave the drama half way through because it has a nice storyline but the depictions on psychological disorders has me on edge sometimes. I can't expect for the writers and director of the drama to be experts in psychology which is why I’m overlooking many things and enjoying the storyline. Still I've watched many psychology Kdramas before and they did a great job in the research, so comparing is inevitable. Getting back to the point, I can't overlook where the storyline is heading.

Antisocial Personality Disorder- commonly known by the terms of sociopathy (raised) and psychopathy (born), it's an irregularity on the brain where neurons are lacking to reproduce hormones that produce emotions. Speaking it's literally a disorder about a lack of emotions- lack of remorse, empathy, etc. There is no cure for this disorder, a person cannot be cured but can become high functioning. High functioning meaning they can live a perfectly normal live between society with the help of therapy, still their brain is structured differently though they can learn how to act according to the situation, they won't feel how the rest feels about the same situation. For example in a funeral they can act accordingly, but that doesn't mean they will necessarily feel sad.

It's important to point out that having this disorder doesn't make anyone a bad person. The majority of assesins and bad people in the world Do Not have this disorder. The guy/girl who played with your emotions and didn't care about you most likely doesn't have this condition either. Society has misinformed and have depicted this disorder with a negative and scary connotation, especially the film industry. High functioning people can live a normal live and won't “harm, kill or manipulate” you as shown in the movies and series, their brain just works differently and lacks emotions.

However, showing a series where they show a person with this disorder falling in love leads to misinformation also. As already said this condition is literally about lacking emotions. Love is a strong feeling, even people without said condition have only fallen in love once in their entire lifetime and others never have. Love requires too much empathy. The moment you love someone, they become the person you feel most empathy for. So people with this condition can't fall in love. They have trouble processing simple feelings, so complex feelings won't happen. This doesn't mean they can't carry on a relationship, but as a couple you would have to understand that they can't fall in love with you, still high functionings know how to act accordingly in a relationship.

I'm still at episode 4 which may be too soon to be commenting lol. If she does fall in love and the writers did their research, I'm leaning towards a wrong diagnosis was given to her and she probably has something else that will become more clear as episodes go by.

Adding to this do not romanticize mental disorders, do not romanticize posessiveness and do not romanticize toxic relationship . DO NOT let people treat you less than good and nice. You aren't someone else's object.

Personally, I liked Itaewon Class better. Both k-dramas released this year are very well planned out. They both have a great cast, production value, unique plots and tons of popularity. One thing that I loved about both shows is that they are not afraid to touch on societal issues that need to be discussed more frequently, especially in Asian countries.

![Image 55](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-a86de0af9de448e526479afc996ea24d-lq)

In terms of Itaewon Class, the unpredictability played a huge factor in the distinctive plot. The storyline talks about this young man, Park Sae-ro-yi, facing difficult challenges in life without giving up his righteousness and while starting his own business. It’s hard to predict what new challenges will come his way. Right when you think he will finally succeed and get with his longtime love interest, more roadblocks are piled in front of him and the tables turn once again.

Itaewon Class is actually based on a Webtoon which is not necessarily good or bad. It explains why there is more conflict and action in the show compared to others. That being said, people who do not watch kdrama can enjoy the well written plot as well.

There are many themes. Apart from the main theme of staying strong despite adversities, there are multiple minor hidden themes. For instance, as Kim To-ni is declined from a club for being black, we see some racial injustice prevalent in Korea. By featuring these issues in popular shows, it can hopefully help spread more awareness. After watching this drama, it feels like there are lessons you can take away and apply in your own life.

I have to admit that the Cast in both dramas are nicely selected. Park Seo-joon from Itaewon Class did a great job in portraying his protagonist role. Aside from Lee Joo-young (transgender chef), Kim Dong-hee (illegitimate son) and Park Bo-gum (guest), the other actors are generally not as popular. Disregarding fame, all the actors were quite skilled, allowing the characters to contrast each other perfectly.

![Image 56](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-2abe567c2d131ed8c7c633e46b41b306-lq)

I’m not sure if this is just my experience, but the immense TikTok hype surrounding It’s Okay to Not Be Okay made me enjoy the drama less. Usually, the kdrama side of social media platforms is not too popular, but when It’s Okay to Not Be Okay was released, all social platforms were praising this particular drama. It might be because this is many people’s first k-drama. Because, I started watching the show immediately after it was released, nobody knew about it; However, after hearing about everyone else’s opinion, the drama felt extremely hyped near the finale. I would still recommend it though.

It ultimately comes down to which genre of show you prefer more. Itaewon Class is more business, competition, values, food and friendship themed while It’s Okay to Not Be Okay is geared towards romance, psychology, trauma and comedy.
