There is a fundamental Korean concept called “Han” 한 (in Hangul). Han is a very complicated emotion to accurately define in English. Some would say it’s impossible to understand if you’re not Korean. The best definition that I can give as someone who has studied Korean language and culture extensively is “a profound mix of grief, longing, resentment, anger, injustice, sadness, and regret”. Han is deeply embedded in Korean culture. The modern definition of Han is largely influenced by the Japanese occupation of Korea from 1910–1945. Families were torn apart politically and geographically. Some elders in Korea still have family in North Korea whom they haven’t seen since the war. It’s truly heart breaking. Han also contains a deep sorrow within it. The feeling of knowing that something isn’t or never will be resolved. This was passed down as a form of generational trauma. Koreans also have a culture-bound mental illness called “Hwabyung” 화병 which literally translates to “anger illness”. Some have claimed people have died from it.

With that in mind, you can see why crying and sadness has become part of many Korean drama storylines. The people who wrote the scripts, produced, directed, acted, etc. in these dramas and movies probably had parents and/or grandparents that lived through the devastation that was brutal colonial rule and post-war Korea. Art can imitate life or aspects of life. This is also why Korea has a huge ballad song catalog.

On another side note, but still relevant I think, is the grieving/funerary culture in Korea. People are encouraged to cry and wail loudly because there is a belief that the tears and cries of the living family members will assist the soul to heaven/afterlife, and because if you don’t show a lot of emotion, people might think you didn’t love whoever it was that passed away very much. This is especially the case if you are the offspring of someone who died. It’s seen as an act of filial piety to grieve openly and loudly. This is in stark contrast to the West (where I’m from) and in Anglo-Saxon, Western European based communities, the conduct at funerals is one of showing perceived strength through/in sadness , silence, remembrance, and reflection. If you cry and wail like Koreans do at funerals in Anglo-Saxon/Western funerals, you’ll be seen as an attention seeker, like you’re trying to prove a point that you’re the saddest person there when clearly everyone there will be sad already. It could also make things worse in an already emotionally unstable life changing event. So yeah, culture differences there too.

Koreans are more emotionally honest, and get headstrong/emotional pretty easily whether it’s something euphoric or upsetting, minor or major. Crying is seen as an act of devotion or care to the person you are crying for/to. It’s exaggerated in dramas for entertainment of course, but nevertheless the sadness and Han roots run deep, and crying in dramas is one manifestation of that.

Why do people like Korean dramas?

Here are some of my reasons:

*   Korean dramas last only one season, usually. This means the season was designed to produce a good story. Not too long; not too short.
*   Korean characters are very well developed. Even the supporting characters have stories to tell. This tends to draw the audience further into the drama.
*   They do romance better than American dramas. With Koreans, love is about a solid relationship where each will stand with the other. It’s not focused on sex like American dramas tend to be.
*   They are very good at comedy and they are very open about things Americans won’t talk about in their dramas, like dog poop and farts, even female ones.
*   The good Korean characters are heavily respectful of others. Of course, the bad characters tend to kick those below them and kiss the ass of those above them. However, this problem is often part of the drama, itself. The bad characters never really win, though.
*   The good Korean characters are very self-reflective about what they may have done that caused something to go wrong. This honesty and sincerity of character is a real draw on viewers, making it possible for them to empathize with them.
*   Music score. The songs or music in the background are almost always good. They weave the drama around you like a blanket, especially in romantic comedies.
*   Korean dramas are almost always partly about family - the effect good or bad on the characters. Koreans are far more family-oriented in almost everything they do when compared to American culture. I like that a lot. Of course, their dramas will show overbearing parents who abuse their children but that is only part of the drama to show how what could have been a good relationship can be so bad.
*   The good Korean characters reframe from using violence whenever they can. They hold it in, and I think that’s better, even though my American English/Irish self many times would have punched the bad character! The Koreans are so much smarter about not adding fuel to someone’s hate and anger.

There are many more reasons but I would have to go into more detail, and most people don’t want that. I just like them so much better than our hard-ass, uncaring, I will kill you American dramas. When we do romance we rarely get it right.

Anyway, Korean dramas are my primary source of entertainment now, along with dramas from China, Taiwan, and Japan. I’m amazed that having the ancestry of the English and Irish that I prefer the Asian culture, the good part of it so much better. At least, for me.

Trailer

*   Amazing Acting

One of the first things I noticed was the acting in this drama. Both lead actors are extremely versatile and from watching bloopers, you can see how they are really pretty different people in person.

![Image 60](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-d6ab3309c624ef1e3354a92d6da49ab2-lq)

![Image 61](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-fa7f4e99099f19023c88305d6efe6b79-lq)

Kim Soo-hyun is the main lead who is already pretty popular from his previous work such as My Love from the Star, Dream High, Real (movie), Moon Embracing the Sun, and Hotel Del Luna. I was personally surprised about his cameo as a delivery guy in Crash Landing on You because his personalities and looks were very diverse. In the drama, he can get the audience quite emotional in certain scenes. His pain is also very evident.

![Image 62](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-2677a3f8687d7c10624582841d6db663-lq)

![Image 63](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-8bbc98cd4f55e72b36643e92950c05ce-lq)

Seo Ye-ji is the female lead who has an antisocial personality disorder. She is meant to be a cruel antagonist-like character, but she is actually very sweet in person. She has also gained some fame form her dramas S ave Me, Hwarang: The Poet Warrior Youth, Another Miss Oh, and Lawless Lawyer. To me, her character in the drama is a mix of Jo-Yi Seo from Itaewon Class and Wol-joo from Mystic Pop-up Bar; both of which are great developed characters as well.

*   Unique Plot

THIS IS DEFINITELY NOT YOUR TYPICAL ROM-COM K-DRAMA. None of the scenes are cliché at all and there are already many unpredictable moments where you think things would have gone the opposite way. This drama dives deep into the emotional wounds of both characters and is a very emotion-based show in general. The setting is between hospitals and crowds of paparazzi which creates a lot of extra drama. Props to the writers for such a unique plot. This is much more than a simple romance.

![Image 64](https://qph.cf2.quoracdn.net/main-qimg-7234b2205dbfd977f86bb32426a99a52-lq)

*   Touches on Mental Illness

I have heard that in South Korea, mental health is not talked about openly and is generally frowned upon. Despite that, this show is able to touch on mental illness in a more positive light. It shows how people deal with problems differently. Moon Kang-tae’s (male lead) older brother is on the spectrum and it brings to light the difficulties in everyday life for him including panic attacks and public judgement.

Because the story includes a well-known children’s book author, they occasionally incorporate dark-themed illustrations. The k-drama starts off with a fictional short story with beautiful drawings. Although this may seem childish, the stories are fairly dark and eerie to the point where some people get scared.

# K-Drama Review : It’s Okay to Not Be Okay

![Image 2: K-Drama Review : It’s Okay to Not Be Okay](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/images.jpg?resize=350%2C500&ssl=1)**It's Okay to Not be Okay****Published by**[Netflix](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/books/publishers/netflix/) on June 20 - August 9, 2020   
**Genres:**[Romance](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/books/genres/romance/), [Drama](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/books/genres/drama/)  
[Barnes & Noble](http://www.barnesandnoble.com/s/?store=allproducts&keyword=It%27s+Okay+to+Not+be+Okay),[or Bookshop.org](https://bookshop.org/search?keywords=It%27s+Okay+to+Not+be+Okay)  
[Find on Goodreads](https://www.goodreads.com/search?utf8=%E2%9C%93&query=It%27s+Okay+to+Not+be+Okay)  
![Image 3: three-stars](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/plugins/ultimate-book-blogger/assets/images/stars/circle_blue/three-stars.png?ssl=1)  

> A road to emotional healing opens up for an antisocial children's book author (Seo Ye-ji) and an employee (Kim Soo-hyun) in a psychiatric hospital.

_It’s Okay to Not Be Oka_ y is a K-drama that tells the story of two brothers, Moon Gang-tae and his older brother, Moon Sang-tae. Due to the loss of their mother at a young age, Moon Gang-tae becomes the sole caretaker of Sang-tae, who has Autism Spectrum Disorder. As Sang-tae was the only one who witnessed their mother’s murder, he has traumatic nightmares inexplicably having to do with butterflies attacking him—and the two have to be ready to pack up and leave at a moment’s notice in order for Sang-tae to feel safe again and for their life to be livable. Before their next move, the brothers meet Ko Mun-yeong, Sang-tae’s favorite children’s book author, and she and Gang-tae develop a romantic relationship. She too, is not without her own personal mental health issues and trauma. Without a doubt, _It’s Okay Not to be Okay_ is at its best when portraying mental illnesses, healing, and the bonds between brothers. Unfortunately, when the show dives more into the mystery surrounding the murder of Gang-tae and Sang-tae’s mother, it borders on mediocre.

[![Image 4](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/brothers2-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/brothers2.png?ssl=1) Sang-tae and Gang-tae.
What I liked the most about _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay_ is the character of Sang-tae. Sang-tae is not relegated to the role of a side character or any kind of plot device, as so many characters with Autism Spectrum Disorder are. Instead, he is an integral part of the show, and his thoughts, feelings, and needs are shown as extremely important to everyone. In fact, Ko Mun-yeong essentially has to gain Sang-tae’s approval before officially dating Gang-tae. This is a main sticking point of the show, as Sang-tae is used to his younger brother basing his entire life around him and his needs. It’s really beautiful how these three characters form a “found” family over time—one that not only accepts each other’s mental health issues, but loves each other for them. I feel like Ko Mun-yeoung and Gang-tae’s relationship is more powerful because of having to go slowly to gain Sang-tae’s acceptance and because of overcoming their own personal issues.

[![Image 6](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/twobrothers-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/twobrothers.png?ssl=1) Moon Gang-tae took care of Sang-tae on his own from an extremely young age.
Gang-tae for example, has never been able to date, let alone put down roots anywhere. Every year, he packs up, quits his job, and moves to avoid Sang-tae’s butterflies. I cannot imagine the emotional toll this alone takes on a person, especially since he’s been caring for his brother all alone from a very young age. What’s more, is that he also works in psychiatric hospitals as an orderly/caregiver, as he never was able to continue his education after his mother died. Most of his trauma also stems from the fact that his mother treated him like he was only born to take care of and to protect Sang-tae. All this emotional turmoil turns him into someone who thinks his wants and needs are selfish and unimportant. As such, Gang-tae is completely unable to express how he really feels and masks his emotions as not to upset his older brother.

[![Image 8](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/itsokaytonotbeokaybook-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/itsokaytonotbeokaybook.png?ssl=1) The show features a lot of illustrations from Ko Mun-yeong’s children’s books.
Ko Mun-yeong is Gang-tae’s love interest, and Sang-tae’s eventual best friend. _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay_ remarks off-handedly that she has antisocial personality disorder, a pretty serious mental health diagnosis which is defined as a complete disregard for others, though I don’t know if that’s her actual diagnosis. Regardless, Ko Mun-yeong doesn’t seem to have many worries for the thoughts and feelings of others, doing whatever she wants on whim, with no thought of the consequences. This means that when she decides she likes something or someone, in the case of Gang-tae, she goes after it with every fiber of her being and boy, do antics ensue. She’s absolutely wild and I immediately loved her. Not only is she beautiful, but so are the children’s books she writes—her only way of communicating her true feelings to the world. In fact, all of the episodes share a title with one of her books or another famous fairytale and it is her books that allow her to bond with Sang-tae._(Sidenote: I would 100% read any of her Tim Burton-esque books, and apparently they are actually on sale somewhere in South Korea. If only I could read Hangul.)_

[![Image 10](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/tears-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/tears.png?ssl=1)

It’s really beautiful how Sang-tae, Gang-tae, and Ko Mun-yeong manage to work past all of their traumas together. The show does a great job sensitively reflecting each of their emotional traumas from childhood and how they shaped them into the adults they are. And as it turns out, these three have more shared trauma than they initially thought, and that’s where _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay_ loses its way. It turns out Ko Mun-yeong’s mother, who traumatized her so much that she sees her as a ghost during her sleep paralysis, is View Spoiler » the murderer of Sang-tae and Gang-tae’s mother. To top it off, she’s been moonlighting as the head nurse at Ok Psychiatric Hospital, where all three of them work. The show brazenly and arbitrarily suggests that the reason Ko Mun-yeong and Sang-tae don’t recognize her, is because “plastic surgery exists” and “she looks so different.” « Hide Spoiler It’s a huge stretch, and completely unbelievable. This all comes to light in the final episodes of the show to try and tear a happy Ko Mun-yeong and Gang-tae apart, and it all just feels really contrived and unnecessary. I think the show should’ve simply spent more time developing its side characters in the psychiatric ward, or the second leads (who I honestly didn’t care much at all about), instead of going down this weird path. This bizarre twist, if you can call something so poorly written and explained a twist, really ruined the whole show for me.

[![Image 12](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/komunyeong-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/komunyeong.png?ssl=1)

My only other problem with _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay,_ was that in the beginning of the show Ko Mun-yeong was walking around almost stabbing people in the eye with pens, pushing them down the stairs, and slicing someone with a knife. She was clearly off the rails, and the show really dials down her behavioral issues when she falls in love with Gang-tae, almost as if love “cures” her and makes her magically care about the well-being of others. This could be a dangerous message to send people about mental health. I wish It’s _Okay Not to be Okay_ would’ve shown her getting therapy or something of the sort, though Sang-tae’s therapy didn’t really seem legitimate either. He literally sits down with the director of Ok Psychiatric Hospital one time for roughly five minutes in a single episode, and somehow the doctor magically convinces him to confront his years-long fear of butterflies.

[![Image 14](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/stab-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/stab.png?ssl=1) Ko Mun-yeong stabs Moon Gang-tae the first time she meets him.
Regardless, it concerned me that not only did _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay choose_ not show her working on her issues under the guidance of a mental health professional, but also that a psychiatric hospital hired her with no concern for how her own personality disorder/conditions would effect their patients. And it does, she makes one patient faint, and another cry from her harsh words. It’s mind-boggling that they even hired her, as she tried to stab another, violent patient on her very first visit, but ends up slicing Gang-tae when he prevents her from doing so. At they very least, hiring her seems like a bad idea, at worst, it seems like medical malpractice and a lawsuit.

[![Image 16](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/sang-tae-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/sang-tae.png?ssl=1)

I also had trouble believing parts of the portrayal’s of Sang-tae’s mental health. I was surprised that Sang-tae had as little of a set routine as he did, occasionally working as a part-timer in a pizza shop, others going to school, and sometimes lived on his own for the night and was able to cook for himself with no issue, despite being prone to episodes of panic. I was a Psychology major in college for a semester and took a course on “The Exceptional Child,” which spent a lot of time on Autism Spectrum Disorder, so I think I might know a tiny bit more than the average person, but I am by no means an expert. However, with what little I do know, I just didn’t think Sang-tae seemed to be high functioning enough to be able to do all these things without supervision or without accident or harm, especially with his sporadic episodes that leave him unable to cope at all and require him to self-isolate.

But I guess the romance and plot had to move forward sometimes, and for the latter especially, show had to get Gang-tae and Mun-yeong alone, so they made this happen whether it was realistic or not for Sang-tae’s overall well-being. Likewise, the psychiatric patients are seen walking around with little to no supervision, having all sorts of personal stuff in their rooms, and it just didn’t seem like a very accurate portrayal of a psychiatric hospital to me. I wish the show had committed a bit more to realism. While it’s okay to not be okay, it’s not so okay to show unrealistic treatments for mental health.

[![Image 18: Sang-tae And Ko Mun](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/besties-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/besties.png?ssl=1)

Despite these issues, I do think the show does an overall solid job of its portrayal of Sang-tae, as I said before. Other shows have a tendency to sideline characters with similar conditions, to not spend as much time developing them, and to sadly, use them as plot devices. I love that _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay_ made Sang-tae a main character as important as Gang-tae and Ko Mun Yeong. And the actor who portrays Sang-tae, Oh Jung-se, does an absolutely phenomenal job! He takes care to portray his character’s struggles of making eye contact and having tics. Likewise, the actress playing Ko Mun-yeong, Seo Ye-ji, blew me away. Viewers can literally see her thoughts playing across her face, and she does a great job balancing portraying a confident, strong woman who is also incredibly vulnerable. For me, the weakest link out of these main three actors on the show, was surprisingly Kim Soo-Hyun, who plays Gang-tae. I don’t know if it was simply because he was playing a character who hides his true feelings, but a lot of the times, I had no idea what was going on through his head. Unfortunately, this was really noticeable in contrast to the other main actor and actress. The character’s emotional outbursts, when they did happen, seemed very random as result of his inability to portray the minute details of emotions. I simply didn’t care for this portrayal as much as the portrayals of the other characters.

[![Image 20](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/foundfamily-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/foundfamily.png?ssl=1) Gang-tae, Mun-yeong, and Sang-tae form a “found” family.
Overall, I did enjoy _It’s Okay to Not be Okay._ It was very entertaining for the most part, making me laugh out loud at times, and sharing a lot if its theme through the interesting medium of children’s books. Obviously, the show did try to handle the delicate mental health of its characters with sensitivity, even though it wasn’t always a very realistic portrayal of the healing process, etc.. I really enjoyed the unique relationship between the three main characters, and loved the acting of two of these leads. However, I definitely lost interest in the show when it dealt with the mystery surrounding the murder of Gang-tae and Sang-tae’s mother and I found myself on my phone a lot browsing the internet instead of paying full attention to the show during these parts. If viewers want to watch a K-drama dealing with mental health and that has a well-done twist, I recommend they watch [_It’s Okay, That’s Love_](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/watch-kdramas-its-okay-thats-love-review/) instead.

The unfortunate plot twist re the death of the mother can be ignored IMO bc there is so much ground gained concerning the exploration of mental health by producing a series such as this one. No one and I mean no one, talks about mental health. Even less so is it portrayed in the entertainment world, so we will give that twist a miss, just move on, appreciate this monumental auspicious undertaking.

This series did more for bringing the real lives of people suffering from mental health challenges into the light than 99% of all else that’s available in US, European and Korean entertainment.

Having reached the end of the series, it will be sad not “spending time” with these lovely characters, Moon Sang Tae (will miss him the most!), Ko Moon Young and Moon Gang Tae.

Bravo!

# K-Drama Review : It’s Okay to Not Be Okay

![Image 2: K-Drama Review : It’s Okay to Not Be Okay](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/images.jpg?resize=350%2C500&ssl=1)**It's Okay to Not be Okay****Published by**[Netflix](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/books/publishers/netflix/) on June 20 - August 9, 2020   
**Genres:**[Romance](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/books/genres/romance/), [Drama](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/books/genres/drama/)  
[Barnes & Noble](http://www.barnesandnoble.com/s/?store=allproducts&keyword=It%27s+Okay+to+Not+be+Okay),[or Bookshop.org](https://bookshop.org/search?keywords=It%27s+Okay+to+Not+be+Okay)  
[Find on Goodreads](https://www.goodreads.com/search?utf8=%E2%9C%93&query=It%27s+Okay+to+Not+be+Okay)  
![Image 3: three-stars](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/plugins/ultimate-book-blogger/assets/images/stars/circle_blue/three-stars.png?ssl=1)  

> A road to emotional healing opens up for an antisocial children's book author (Seo Ye-ji) and an employee (Kim Soo-hyun) in a psychiatric hospital.

_It’s Okay to Not Be Oka_ y is a K-drama that tells the story of two brothers, Moon Gang-tae and his older brother, Moon Sang-tae. Due to the loss of their mother at a young age, Moon Gang-tae becomes the sole caretaker of Sang-tae, who has Autism Spectrum Disorder. As Sang-tae was the only one who witnessed their mother’s murder, he has traumatic nightmares inexplicably having to do with butterflies attacking him—and the two have to be ready to pack up and leave at a moment’s notice in order for Sang-tae to feel safe again and for their life to be livable. Before their next move, the brothers meet Ko Mun-yeong, Sang-tae’s favorite children’s book author, and she and Gang-tae develop a romantic relationship. She too, is not without her own personal mental health issues and trauma. Without a doubt, _It’s Okay Not to be Okay_ is at its best when portraying mental illnesses, healing, and the bonds between brothers. Unfortunately, when the show dives more into the mystery surrounding the murder of Gang-tae and Sang-tae’s mother, it borders on mediocre.

[![Image 4](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/brothers2-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/brothers2.png?ssl=1) Sang-tae and Gang-tae.
What I liked the most about _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay_ is the character of Sang-tae. Sang-tae is not relegated to the role of a side character or any kind of plot device, as so many characters with Autism Spectrum Disorder are. Instead, he is an integral part of the show, and his thoughts, feelings, and needs are shown as extremely important to everyone. In fact, Ko Mun-yeong essentially has to gain Sang-tae’s approval before officially dating Gang-tae. This is a main sticking point of the show, as Sang-tae is used to his younger brother basing his entire life around him and his needs. It’s really beautiful how these three characters form a “found” family over time—one that not only accepts each other’s mental health issues, but loves each other for them. I feel like Ko Mun-yeoung and Gang-tae’s relationship is more powerful because of having to go slowly to gain Sang-tae’s acceptance and because of overcoming their own personal issues.

[![Image 6](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/twobrothers-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/twobrothers.png?ssl=1) Moon Gang-tae took care of Sang-tae on his own from an extremely young age.
Gang-tae for example, has never been able to date, let alone put down roots anywhere. Every year, he packs up, quits his job, and moves to avoid Sang-tae’s butterflies. I cannot imagine the emotional toll this alone takes on a person, especially since he’s been caring for his brother all alone from a very young age. What’s more, is that he also works in psychiatric hospitals as an orderly/caregiver, as he never was able to continue his education after his mother died. Most of his trauma also stems from the fact that his mother treated him like he was only born to take care of and to protect Sang-tae. All this emotional turmoil turns him into someone who thinks his wants and needs are selfish and unimportant. As such, Gang-tae is completely unable to express how he really feels and masks his emotions as not to upset his older brother.

[![Image 8](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/itsokaytonotbeokaybook-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/itsokaytonotbeokaybook.png?ssl=1) The show features a lot of illustrations from Ko Mun-yeong’s children’s books.
Ko Mun-yeong is Gang-tae’s love interest, and Sang-tae’s eventual best friend. _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay_ remarks off-handedly that she has antisocial personality disorder, a pretty serious mental health diagnosis which is defined as a complete disregard for others, though I don’t know if that’s her actual diagnosis. Regardless, Ko Mun-yeong doesn’t seem to have many worries for the thoughts and feelings of others, doing whatever she wants on whim, with no thought of the consequences. This means that when she decides she likes something or someone, in the case of Gang-tae, she goes after it with every fiber of her being and boy, do antics ensue. She’s absolutely wild and I immediately loved her. Not only is she beautiful, but so are the children’s books she writes—her only way of communicating her true feelings to the world. In fact, all of the episodes share a title with one of her books or another famous fairytale and it is her books that allow her to bond with Sang-tae._(Sidenote: I would 100% read any of her Tim Burton-esque books, and apparently they are actually on sale somewhere in South Korea. If only I could read Hangul.)_

[![Image 10](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/tears-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/tears.png?ssl=1)

It’s really beautiful how Sang-tae, Gang-tae, and Ko Mun-yeong manage to work past all of their traumas together. The show does a great job sensitively reflecting each of their emotional traumas from childhood and how they shaped them into the adults they are. And as it turns out, these three have more shared trauma than they initially thought, and that’s where _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay_ loses its way. It turns out Ko Mun-yeong’s mother, who traumatized her so much that she sees her as a ghost during her sleep paralysis, is View Spoiler » the murderer of Sang-tae and Gang-tae’s mother. To top it off, she’s been moonlighting as the head nurse at Ok Psychiatric Hospital, where all three of them work. The show brazenly and arbitrarily suggests that the reason Ko Mun-yeong and Sang-tae don’t recognize her, is because “plastic surgery exists” and “she looks so different.” « Hide Spoiler It’s a huge stretch, and completely unbelievable. This all comes to light in the final episodes of the show to try and tear a happy Ko Mun-yeong and Gang-tae apart, and it all just feels really contrived and unnecessary. I think the show should’ve simply spent more time developing its side characters in the psychiatric ward, or the second leads (who I honestly didn’t care much at all about), instead of going down this weird path. This bizarre twist, if you can call something so poorly written and explained a twist, really ruined the whole show for me.

[![Image 12](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/komunyeong-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/komunyeong.png?ssl=1)

My only other problem with _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay,_ was that in the beginning of the show Ko Mun-yeong was walking around almost stabbing people in the eye with pens, pushing them down the stairs, and slicing someone with a knife. She was clearly off the rails, and the show really dials down her behavioral issues when she falls in love with Gang-tae, almost as if love “cures” her and makes her magically care about the well-being of others. This could be a dangerous message to send people about mental health. I wish It’s _Okay Not to be Okay_ would’ve shown her getting therapy or something of the sort, though Sang-tae’s therapy didn’t really seem legitimate either. He literally sits down with the director of Ok Psychiatric Hospital one time for roughly five minutes in a single episode, and somehow the doctor magically convinces him to confront his years-long fear of butterflies.

[![Image 14](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/stab-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/stab.png?ssl=1) Ko Mun-yeong stabs Moon Gang-tae the first time she meets him.
Regardless, it concerned me that not only did _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay choose_ not show her working on her issues under the guidance of a mental health professional, but also that a psychiatric hospital hired her with no concern for how her own personality disorder/conditions would effect their patients. And it does, she makes one patient faint, and another cry from her harsh words. It’s mind-boggling that they even hired her, as she tried to stab another, violent patient on her very first visit, but ends up slicing Gang-tae when he prevents her from doing so. At they very least, hiring her seems like a bad idea, at worst, it seems like medical malpractice and a lawsuit.

[![Image 16](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/sang-tae-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/sang-tae.png?ssl=1)

I also had trouble believing parts of the portrayal’s of Sang-tae’s mental health. I was surprised that Sang-tae had as little of a set routine as he did, occasionally working as a part-timer in a pizza shop, others going to school, and sometimes lived on his own for the night and was able to cook for himself with no issue, despite being prone to episodes of panic. I was a Psychology major in college for a semester and took a course on “The Exceptional Child,” which spent a lot of time on Autism Spectrum Disorder, so I think I might know a tiny bit more than the average person, but I am by no means an expert. However, with what little I do know, I just didn’t think Sang-tae seemed to be high functioning enough to be able to do all these things without supervision or without accident or harm, especially with his sporadic episodes that leave him unable to cope at all and require him to self-isolate.

But I guess the romance and plot had to move forward sometimes, and for the latter especially, show had to get Gang-tae and Mun-yeong alone, so they made this happen whether it was realistic or not for Sang-tae’s overall well-being. Likewise, the psychiatric patients are seen walking around with little to no supervision, having all sorts of personal stuff in their rooms, and it just didn’t seem like a very accurate portrayal of a psychiatric hospital to me. I wish the show had committed a bit more to realism. While it’s okay to not be okay, it’s not so okay to show unrealistic treatments for mental health.

[![Image 18: Sang-tae And Ko Mun](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/besties-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/besties.png?ssl=1)

Despite these issues, I do think the show does an overall solid job of its portrayal of Sang-tae, as I said before. Other shows have a tendency to sideline characters with similar conditions, to not spend as much time developing them, and to sadly, use them as plot devices. I love that _It’s Okay to Not Be Okay_ made Sang-tae a main character as important as Gang-tae and Ko Mun Yeong. And the actor who portrays Sang-tae, Oh Jung-se, does an absolutely phenomenal job! He takes care to portray his character’s struggles of making eye contact and having tics. Likewise, the actress playing Ko Mun-yeong, Seo Ye-ji, blew me away. Viewers can literally see her thoughts playing across her face, and she does a great job balancing portraying a confident, strong woman who is also incredibly vulnerable. For me, the weakest link out of these main three actors on the show, was surprisingly Kim Soo-Hyun, who plays Gang-tae. I don’t know if it was simply because he was playing a character who hides his true feelings, but a lot of the times, I had no idea what was going on through his head. Unfortunately, this was really noticeable in contrast to the other main actor and actress. The character’s emotional outbursts, when they did happen, seemed very random as result of his inability to portray the minute details of emotions. I simply didn’t care for this portrayal as much as the portrayals of the other characters.

[![Image 20](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/foundfamily-1024x576.png)](https://i0.wp.com/bloggingwithdragons.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/foundfamily.png?ssl=1) Gang-tae, Mun-yeong, and Sang-tae form a “found” family.
Overall, I did enjoy _It’s Okay to Not be Okay._ It was very entertaining for the most part, making me laugh out loud at times, and sharing a lot if its theme through the interesting medium of children’s books. Obviously, the show did try to handle the delicate mental health of its characters with sensitivity, even though it wasn’t always a very realistic portrayal of the healing process, etc.. I really enjoyed the unique relationship between the three main characters, and loved the acting of two of these leads. However, I definitely lost interest in the show when it dealt with the mystery surrounding the murder of Gang-tae and Sang-tae’s mother and I found myself on my phone a lot browsing the internet instead of paying full attention to the show during these parts. If viewers want to watch a K-drama dealing with mental health and that has a well-done twist, I recommend they watch [_It’s Okay, That’s Love_](https://bloggingwithdragons.com/watch-kdramas-its-okay-thats-love-review/) instead.

## Plot Synopsis by AsianWiki Staff ©

A story about a man employed in a psychiatric ward and a woman, with an antisocial personality disorder, who is a popular writer of children's books.

Moon Kang-Tae ([Kim Soo-Hyun](https://asianwiki.com/Kim_Soo-Hyun_(1988) "Kim Soo-Hyun (1988)")) works in the psychiatric ward. His job is to write down the patients' conditions and to deal with unexpected situations, like if patients fight or they run away. He only earns about 1.8 million won (~$1,600 USD) a month. The woman ([Seo Yea-Ji](https://asianwiki.com/Seo_Yea-Ji "Seo Yea-Ji")) is a popular writer of children's literature, but she is extremely selfish, arrogant and rude.

## Plot Synopsis by AsianWiki Staff ©

A story about a man employed in a psychiatric ward and a woman, with an antisocial personality disorder, who is a popular writer of children's books.

Moon Kang-Tae ([Kim Soo-Hyun](https://asianwiki.com/Kim_Soo-Hyun_(1988) "Kim Soo-Hyun (1988)")) works in the psychiatric ward. His job is to write down the patients' conditions and to deal with unexpected situations, like if patients fight or they run away. He only earns about 1.8 million won (~$1,600 USD) a month. The woman ([Seo Yea-Ji](https://asianwiki.com/Seo_Yea-Ji "Seo Yea-Ji")) is a popular writer of children's literature, but she is extremely selfish, arrogant and rude.

_**It's Okay to Not Be Okay**_ ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"):사이코지만 괜찮아) is a 2020 [South Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_drama "Korean drama")[romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_film "Romance film")[comedy drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_drama "Comedy drama") television series written by Jo Yong, directed by [Park Shin-woo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Shin-woo "Park Shin-woo"), and starring [Kim Soo-hyun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Soo-hyun "Kim Soo-hyun"), [Seo Yea-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seo_Yea-ji "Seo Yea-ji"), and [Oh Jung-se](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oh_Jung-se "Oh Jung-se"). The series follows Ko Moon-young, an [antisocial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-social_behaviour "Anti-social behaviour") children's book writer who moves to her hometown to pursue her love interest Moon Gang-tae, a [psych ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_hospital "Psychiatric hospital") caretaker, who has dedicated his life to taking care of his autistic older brother Moon Sang-tae. It aired on [tvN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TvN_(South_Korean_TV_channel) "TvN (South Korean TV channel)") from June 20 to August 9, 2020, every Saturday and Sunday at 21:00 ([KST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_South_Korea "Time in South Korea")). It is also available for [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_television "Streaming television") on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") in selected regions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-1)

According to Nielsen Korea, the series recorded an average nationwide TV viewership rating of 5.4%. It was the most popular show of 2020 in the romance genre on Netflix in South Korea.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-:0-2) Critical response were primarily positive; some commentators criticized the writing in the latter half of the series but praised the acting by the cast.

_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ named _It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ one of "The Best International Shows of 2020".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-nytimes-3) At the [57th Baeksang Arts Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/57th_Baeksang_Arts_Awards "57th Baeksang Arts Awards"), it received eight nominations with two wins ([Best Supporting Actor – Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baeksang_Arts_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor_%E2%80%93_Television "Baeksang Arts Award for Best Supporting Actor – Television") and Best Technical Achievement – Television for costume design). It received a nomination at the [49th International Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_International_Emmy_Awards "49th International Emmy Awards") in the [Best TV Movie or Miniseries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Emmy_Award_for_Best_TV_Movie_or_Miniseries "International Emmy Award for Best TV Movie or Miniseries") categories.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Moon Gang-tae lives with his older brother Moon Sang-tae, who has [autism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autism "Autism"). They frequently move from town to town ever since Sang-tae witnessed their mother's murder. Gang-Tae works as a caregiver in a [psychiatric ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_ward "Psychiatric ward") at every place they settle in. While working in a hospital, he meets a famous children's book writer, Ko Moon-young, who is rumored to have [antisocial personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisocial_personality_disorder "Antisocial personality disorder").

Circumstances lead Gang-tae to work at the OK Psychiatric Hospital in the fictional Seongjin City, the same city where they all lived when they were young. Meanwhile, Moon-young forms a romantic obsession for Gang-tae after finding out that their pasts overlap. She follows him to Seongjin, where the trio (including Sang-tae) slowly begins to heal each other's emotional wounds. They discover many secrets, seek comfort from each other, and move forward with their lives.

    *   [Moon Woo-jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_Woo-jin "Moon Woo-jin") as young Moon Gang-tae

An orphaned caregiver working at OK Psychiatric Hospital. While he is empathetic to everyone around him, he struggles with self-esteem as a result of his past experiences and avoids having close relationships with anyone other than his older brother.
*   [Seo Yea-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seo_Yea-ji "Seo Yea-ji") as Ko Mun-yeoung[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cast_seo-5)
    *   Kim Soo-in as young Ko Mun-yeoung

A popular children's book author with [antisocial personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisocial_personality_disorder "Antisocial personality disorder"). She had a troubled childhood and a turbulent relationship with her parents. She develops a romantic obsession over Gang-tae after a coincidental encounter, and often goes to extreme lengths to get his attention.
*   [Oh Jung-se](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oh_Jung-se "Oh Jung-se") as Moon Sang-tae[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cast_oh-6)
    *   [Lee Kyu-sung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kyu-sung "Lee Kyu-sung") as young Moon Sang-tae

Moon Gang-tae's older brother that has [autism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autism "Autism"), who is an aspiring illustrator and a fan of Mun-yeoung. He was the sole witness of his mother's murder, which resulted in his [irrational fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phobia "Phobia") of butterflies, as they remind him of his traumatic experience. His fear develops into nightmares every spring, and forces Gang-tae to move towns with him in order to "run away from the butterflies".

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Production")]

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Development")]

_It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ was planned by [Studio Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Dragon "Studio Dragon"), written by Jo Yong, directed by Park Shin-woo, and produced by [Story TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Story_TV "Story TV") and [Gold Medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Medalist_(company) "Gold Medalist (company)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-10) Jo Yong based the drama on her relationship with a man who had a [personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personality_disorder "Personality disorder").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-12) She developed Moon Sang-tae's character by listening to the stories of people with autistic brothers and referred to the books recommended by the CEO of Bear Better, a social enterprise where people with developmental disabilities work.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-13) Fashion director Cho Sang-kyung managed costumes, while fashion designer [Minju Kim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minju_Kim "Minju Kim") designed some of Ko Moon-young's dresses.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-14)

### Casting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Casting")]

In the second half of 2019, [Kim Soo-hyun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Soo-hyun "Kim Soo-hyun") considered _It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ to be his comeback drama following his [obligatory military enlistment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_South_Korea "Conscription in South Korea"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-15) and his casting was confirmed by his agency in February 2020.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cast_kim-4) At the press conference for the drama, he said that he joined the project after being drawn to its title and Moon Gang-tae's character.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-16) In the same month, [Seo Yea-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seo_Yea-ji "Seo Yea-ji") was confirmed to be cast as Ko Moon-young.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cast_seo-5) In March 2020, veteran actor [Oh Jung-se](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oh_Jung-se "Oh Jung-se") accepted the role of Moon Sang-tae;[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cast_oh-6) when asked about his character at the press conference, he commented that "autism isn't an illness, but something you're born with".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-17)

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Filming")]

The filming was completed on July 31, 2020, without a wrap party out of concerns for the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_South_Korea "COVID-19 pandemic in South Korea").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-18) Filming locations for the drama included Cafe Sanida in [Wonju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonju "Wonju"), [Gangwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangwon_Province_(South_Korea) "Gangwon Province (South Korea)"), which provided the background for the "cursed castle", completed with [CGI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery "Computer-generated imagery") effects,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-19) and Secret Blue Cafe in [Goseong County, Gangwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goseong_County,_Gangwon "Goseong County, Gangwon"), which was transformed into OK Psychiatric Hospital for the shooting using props. Outside locations included streets and beaches in Goseong, as well as locations in [Yangju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangju "Yangju") ([Gyeonggi Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeonggi_Province "Gyeonggi Province")) and [Incheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon "Incheon").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-20) Some of the furniture used in the drama were antiques and 100 to 200 years old.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-21)

### Commercial performance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Commercial performance")]

According to the [big data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_data "Big data") analytics firm [Good Data Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Data_Corporation "Good Data Corporation"), _It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ was the most talked about drama online in South Korea for eight consecutive weeks.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-gd-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-36) It became a hot topic on social media when Oh spent a day with an autistic fan.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-37) It also topped [CJ E&M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CJ_E&M "CJ E&M") and AGB [Nielsen Media Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_Media_Research "Nielsen Media Research")'s Content Power Index (CPI)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-39) report during its eight-week run[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-40) with its highest CPI of 373.2 in the first week of August;[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-41) it was the highest rated tvN drama of 2020 in CPI.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-42) Smart Media Rep (SMR), which distributes [VoD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_on_demand "Video on demand") (video on demand) clips of major broadcasters to online platforms like Naver and YouTube, reported the drama had over 110 million cumulative views as of December 10, 2020.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-43) An analysis performed by SMR found that the majority of viewers were in their 20s.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-44)

[Studio Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Dragon "Studio Dragon") recorded its highest quarterly performance in the second quarter of 2020 with sales of ₩141.4 billion, which was attributed to the growth of overseas sales of major dramas including _It's Okay to Not Be Okay._[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-45)[CJ ENM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CJ_ENM "CJ ENM"), parent company of tvN, found that operating profits for the third quarter of 2020 increased by 17.9% when compared to the same period of 2019, due to an increase in digital-related sales as a response to the COVID-19 pandemic.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-46) Following the popularity of the drama, the outfits worn by Seo Yea-ji garnered attention[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-47) and raised the profile of Korean fashion designers and brands of earrings, handbag and nightwear.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-48)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-49) When the soft toys, nightmare doll (Mang-tae) and dinosaur doll that were used in the drama were put on sale, the site quickly sold out.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-50)

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Critical response")]

_It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ largely received positive critical feedback, primarily for its unique premise, visual storytelling, acting by the cast, and importance given to mental health.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-geek-51) Joan MacDonald of _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ called it "the most visually appealing drama of 2020" and said, "Not only are the actors beautiful, but the drama's graphics, cinematography, and costumes are also gorgeous."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-Forbes-52) Contributors to _[Manila Bulletin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila\_Bulletin "Manila Bulletin")_ considered it "unafraid to introduce fresh elements" with necessary clichés in a romantic K-drama, and praised Moon-young as a "headstrong" and "independent woman".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-mbulletin-53) However, when the series debuted, culture critic Chung Deok-hyun was concerned that Moon-young's "exaggerated words and actions" could decrease viewers' immersion in the drama.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-54) In the Filipino version of _[Cosmopolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmopolitan\_(magazine) "Cosmopolitan (magazine)"),_ Jacinda A. Lopez found that the "messages the drama was relaying are where the beauty truly lies".[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cosmopolitan-55) Rumaiysa M Rahman of _[Prothom Alo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prothom\_Alo "Prothom Alo")_ praised writing that "this drama makes people realise, societies should stop looking at those who seem different."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-prothomalo-56)

John Lui and Jan Lee of _[The Straits Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Straits\_Times "The Straits Times")_ gave the drama a rating of 3.5/5 stars and said that Kim "pull[ed] off a sensitive portrayal of a young man whose life has been derailed by tragedy".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-straits-57)_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")'_ Mike Hale called Seo's performance "mesmerizing" and made the drama work.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-nytimes-3) S. Poorvaja of _[The Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hindu "The Hindu")_, praised Moon-Young as a character "excellently played by Seo Yea-ji", but criticized the writing, saying that "the show could have gone into more nuance – especially after the character was marketed as someone having [Anti-Social Personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisocial_personality_disorder "Antisocial personality disorder")". Poorvaja also said that the show's portrayal of a person with autism spectrum disorder was good, commenting that "Oh Jung-se's Moon Sang-tae is perhaps the show's biggest victory."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-thehindu1-58)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-thehindu2-7) Edmund Lee from _[South China Morning Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South\_China\_Morning\_Post "South China Morning Post")_ gave a rating of 3/5 stars, pointing out that the series would disappoint "detective fiction fans" because of the limited explanation of mystery surrounding the murder.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-SCMP-59) Kim Jae-Ha of _[Teen Vogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen\_Vogue "Teen Vogue")_ described the storyline as "vigorous" and said, "The series finale offers hope and a sense of peace. But it will also make even the most stoic viewers tear up."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-tvogue-60)

#### Sexually inappropriate scenes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Sexually inappropriate scenes")]

The series was criticized on social media and the [Korea Communications Standards Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Communications_Standards_Commission "Korea Communications Standards Commission") received over 50 formal complaints, largely for a scene in which Moon-young overtly stares and touches Gang-tae's body as he gets dressed.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-61) In another scene a male character, who suffers from bipolar disorder and exhibitionism, reveals parts of his body, with his genitals being covered by a drawing of an elephant. Some viewers defended these scenes as ways of expressing the characters' personalities.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-62)

On August 26, 2020, the broadcast censorship body issued a legal sanction to the television series for sexually inappropriate scenes in episode three, judging it to be against the broadcast deliberation regulations. It cited Article 27, on duties of integrity, and Article 30, on gender equality. The subcommission gave the reasoning: "Even considering the fact that they were meant to exaggeratedly express a character's personality, (the scenes in question) show how insensitive the drama's producers are to gender equality in broadcasting content that may belittle a certain gender and hold the possibility to justify sexual harassment and molestation."[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-63)

### Viewership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Viewership")]

_It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ was the most popular show of 2020 on Netflix in South Korea in its romance genre.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-:0-2) It was the most popular Korean drama series on Netflix in Taiwan,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-64) and the "most enduring Korean drama" in Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand, being in Netflix's top 10 list for more than 100 days.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-65) The series was also one of the most popular Korean dramas of 2020 on Netflix in Australia, Hong Kong, India, Japan, and South Africa.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-66)

_It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ aired on tvN, which normally has a relatively smaller audience compared to free-to-air TV/public broadcasters ([KBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Broadcasting_System "Korean Broadcasting System"), [SBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_Broadcasting_System "Seoul Broadcasting System"), [MBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munhwa_Broadcasting_Corporation "Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation"), and [EBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_Broadcasting_System "Educational Broadcasting System")). The series logged 6.1% in viewership for its first episode on Saturday but dropped to 4.7% for the next one.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-67) The series maintained its ratings in 4–6% range throughout its run and received audience acclaim, with its final episode recording 7.4% in nationwide ratings, becoming the "highest viewership rating among tvN dramas" at that point of time.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-68)

Main article: [It's Okay to Not Be Okay (Philippine TV series)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay_(Philippine_TV_series) "It's Okay to Not Be Okay (Philippine TV series)")

A Philippine remake of the series was confirmed by [ABS-CBN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABS-CBN "ABS-CBN") in May 2024.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-107)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-108) It premiered from July 21 to October 17, 2025 on [Kapamilya Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapamilya_Channel "Kapamilya Channel"). The series is also available for [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_television "Streaming television") three days in advance on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") and two days in advance on [iWant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IWant "IWant").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-109)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-110)

_**It's Okay to Not Be Okay**_ ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"):사이코지만 괜찮아) is a 2020 [South Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_drama "Korean drama")[romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_film "Romance film")[comedy drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_drama "Comedy drama") television series written by Jo Yong, directed by [Park Shin-woo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Shin-woo "Park Shin-woo"), and starring [Kim Soo-hyun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Soo-hyun "Kim Soo-hyun"), [Seo Yea-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seo_Yea-ji "Seo Yea-ji"), and [Oh Jung-se](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oh_Jung-se "Oh Jung-se"). The series follows Ko Moon-young, an [antisocial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-social_behaviour "Anti-social behaviour") children's book writer who moves to her hometown to pursue her love interest Moon Gang-tae, a [psych ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_hospital "Psychiatric hospital") caretaker, who has dedicated his life to taking care of his autistic older brother Moon Sang-tae. It aired on [tvN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TvN_(South_Korean_TV_channel) "TvN (South Korean TV channel)") from June 20 to August 9, 2020, every Saturday and Sunday at 21:00 ([KST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_South_Korea "Time in South Korea")). It is also available for [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_television "Streaming television") on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") in selected regions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-1)

According to Nielsen Korea, the series recorded an average nationwide TV viewership rating of 5.4%. It was the most popular show of 2020 in the romance genre on Netflix in South Korea.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-:0-2) Critical response were primarily positive; some commentators criticized the writing in the latter half of the series but praised the acting by the cast.

_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ named _It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ one of "The Best International Shows of 2020".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-nytimes-3) At the [57th Baeksang Arts Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/57th_Baeksang_Arts_Awards "57th Baeksang Arts Awards"), it received eight nominations with two wins ([Best Supporting Actor – Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baeksang_Arts_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor_%E2%80%93_Television "Baeksang Arts Award for Best Supporting Actor – Television") and Best Technical Achievement – Television for costume design). It received a nomination at the [49th International Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_International_Emmy_Awards "49th International Emmy Awards") in the [Best TV Movie or Miniseries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Emmy_Award_for_Best_TV_Movie_or_Miniseries "International Emmy Award for Best TV Movie or Miniseries") categories.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

Moon Gang-tae lives with his older brother Moon Sang-tae, who has [autism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autism "Autism"). They frequently move from town to town ever since Sang-tae witnessed their mother's murder. Gang-Tae works as a caregiver in a [psychiatric ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_ward "Psychiatric ward") at every place they settle in. While working in a hospital, he meets a famous children's book writer, Ko Moon-young, who is rumored to have [antisocial personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisocial_personality_disorder "Antisocial personality disorder").

Circumstances lead Gang-tae to work at the OK Psychiatric Hospital in the fictional Seongjin City, the same city where they all lived when they were young. Meanwhile, Moon-young forms a romantic obsession for Gang-tae after finding out that their pasts overlap. She follows him to Seongjin, where the trio (including Sang-tae) slowly begins to heal each other's emotional wounds. They discover many secrets, seek comfort from each other, and move forward with their lives.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Production")]

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Development")]

_It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ was planned by [Studio Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Dragon "Studio Dragon"), written by Jo Yong, directed by Park Shin-woo, and produced by [Story TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Story_TV "Story TV") and [Gold Medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Medalist_(company) "Gold Medalist (company)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-10) Jo Yong based the drama on her relationship with a man who had a [personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personality_disorder "Personality disorder").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-12) She developed Moon Sang-tae's character by listening to the stories of people with autistic brothers and referred to the books recommended by the CEO of Bear Better, a social enterprise where people with developmental disabilities work.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-13) Fashion director Cho Sang-kyung managed costumes, while fashion designer [Minju Kim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minju_Kim "Minju Kim") designed some of Ko Moon-young's dresses.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-14)

### Casting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Casting")]

In the second half of 2019, [Kim Soo-hyun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Soo-hyun "Kim Soo-hyun") considered _It's Okay to Not Be Okay_ to be his comeback drama following his [obligatory military enlistment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_South_Korea "Conscription in South Korea"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-15) and his casting was confirmed by his agency in February 2020.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cast_kim-4) At the press conference for the drama, he said that he joined the project after being drawn to its title and Moon Gang-tae's character.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-16) In the same month, [Seo Yea-ji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seo_Yea-ji "Seo Yea-ji") was confirmed to be cast as Ko Moon-young.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cast_seo-5) In March 2020, veteran actor [Oh Jung-se](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oh_Jung-se "Oh Jung-se") accepted the role of Moon Sang-tae;[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-cast_oh-6) when asked about his character at the press conference, he commented that "autism isn't an illness, but something you're born with".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-17)

### Filming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=It%27s_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Filming")]

The filming was completed on July 31, 2020, without a wrap party out of concerns for the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_South_Korea "COVID-19 pandemic in South Korea").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-18) Filming locations for the drama included Cafe Sanida in [Wonju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonju "Wonju"), [Gangwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangwon_Province_(South_Korea) "Gangwon Province (South Korea)"), which provided the background for the "cursed castle", completed with [CGI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-generated_imagery "Computer-generated imagery") effects,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-19) and Secret Blue Cafe in [Goseong County, Gangwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goseong_County,_Gangwon "Goseong County, Gangwon"), which was transformed into OK Psychiatric Hospital for the shooting using props. Outside locations included streets and beaches in Goseong, as well as locations in [Yangju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangju "Yangju") ([Gyeonggi Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeonggi_Province "Gyeonggi Province")) and [Incheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incheon "Incheon").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-20) Some of the furniture used in the drama were antiques and 100 to 200 years old.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Okay_to_Not_Be_Okay#cite_note-21)
